If you expected the Milwaukee Brewers to enter the World Series without making any adjustments, you must not have been watching the team this season. Even after sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS and overcoming a red-hot Padres squad in the Division Series, manager Pat Murphy is always finding new ways to keep his opponents on their toes.
The Brewers released their batting order on Friday afternoon, just hours before first pitch. Their updated order will be as follows:
1. Jackson Chourio
2. Jake Bauers
3. Christian Yelich
4. William Contreras
5. Brice Turang
6. Garrett Mitchell
7. Cooper Pratt
8. Sal Frelick
9. David Hamilton
What should we take away from the Milwaukee Brewers' updated batting order for Game 1 of the World Series?
This new-look order should give the Brewers an interesting dynamic of staggering lefty and righty batters, likely in hopes of keeping Game 1 starter Nick Martinez, a righty, out of a consistent rhythm to begin the contest. By moving Contreras to fourth, it sets up Milwaukee's best home run hitter this postseason for a grand slam opportunity, should it arise. Meanwhile, Yelich at the third spot gives the Brew Crew a likely opportunity for some much-needed contact hitting early in the rotation.
It's far from surprising to see first baseman Jake Bauers taking such a firm position near the top of the batting order, as Bauers emerged as one of the most reliable offensive threats on the team, and frankly, in all of baseball. His ability to extend the pitch count and make contact persistently has been a thorn in the sides of pitchers everywhere, so this is likely Murphy's best attempt to extend Martinez's pitch count early.
Meanwhile, Turang slotting back into the fifth spot in the lineup makes sense given his inconsistent production thus far in the postseason. Through eight games, the 26-year-old is hitting just .222 with six hits to seven strikeouts. The good news, however, is that Turang turned a corner in the Dodgers series, logging hits in three of four hits, while scoring a run in each contest.
The end of the lineup should be of interest as well. All year long, Brewers fans grappled with questions over David Hamilton's place in the lineup, but through the postseason, he's certainly proving he belongs. Milwaukee is in serious need of some production late in the order, so all eyes will be on Hamilton, as well as Cooper Pratt and Sal Frelick, to carry that torch.
Overall, this is a wise move by Pat Murphy to make sure his lineup isn't identical to what Tampa Bay was expecting to see. Although the players are the same, a little shake-up in the order might force Martinez and the Rays' defense to think twice, which is all the Brewers can really ask for in a matchup of two teams that are this talented defensively.

The World Series will be historic no matter how it plays out, as neither the Milwaukee Brewers nor the Tampa Bay Rays have ever won a championship.
While the series means a lot to everyone competing, it could be a special moment for former NL MVP Christian Yelich. He’s in his 14th season and will have his first opportunity to play for a World Series title.
One of his biggest supporters over the next few weeks will be his girlfriend, Paige Almendariz.
Here are five interesting facts about their relationship together.
Who Is Almendariz?
Like Yelich, Almendariz is a professional athlete in her own right. She currently plays defender for DC Power in the USL Super League.
The 29-year-old was born and raised in Sacramento, California, and has developed into a successful soccer player. Throughout her career, she has also played for clubs in Portugal, including Benfica and Braga, and won multiple titles. Now, Yelich will try to add a championship of his own.
How Did Almendariz and Yelich First Meet?
The two have kept their relationship relatively private, but they reportedly began dating in late 2025 and made their romance public through social media.
Almendariz has continuously shared photos of herself, Yelich and her dog on several occasions.
Check it out:
They Are Both California Natives
As mentioned, Almendariz is from California, and so is Yelich. He was born and raised in Thousand Oaks and attended Thousand Oaks High School.
However, they grew up roughly 400 miles apart, with West Sacramento, where Almendariz grew up, about a seven-hour drive from Thousand Oaks.
Yelich graduated from high school in 2010, while Almendariz graduated in 2016.
They Were Both Division I College Athletes
Both were Division I athletes, although Yelich took a different path when it came to his college commitment.
Out of high school, he committed to play baseball at the University of Miami, a long way from California. However, after the Florida Marlins drafted him, he elected to sign with the MLB team and turn pro immediately. That decision ultimately worked out, given the career he’s had.
As for Almendariz, she enrolled at UNLV to play college soccer after graduating as the valedictorian of her class, staying relatively close to home.
She was a standout defender for the university from 2016 to 2019 before heading to Portugal in 2020 to sign with Lank Vilaverdense.
They Both Have Athletic Siblings
Athletics run in both families. Yelich’s younger brother, Collin, was drafted by the Atlanta Braves in 2015 and played professional baseball for several years, while his other brother, Cameron, served in the United States Marine Corps.
Almendariz is one of five sisters, and her sister Brittany also played Division I soccer at UNLV as a defender. The two even shared the field when Paige was a freshman.

Another season is coming to a close – the World Series is here. The Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays, both vying for their first championship. Who do we think will win? In how many games? Who will get MVP? Here are our thoughts.
As someone who married into a family of Rays fans and will be in Florida with my wife’s family for Halloween I would love to say the Rays will win in seven and I will watch that game with her family, but it is hard to vote against the Brewers.
They have the better offense. They have the better starting pitching. They have the deeper bullpen. They may even be better defensively. And they are going to be a bit more rested.
Because I will be on an airplane for game six I will say that the Brewers will win in six games.
The fun WSMVP choice would be Aaron Ashby continuing to dominate and taking the award by storm but a reliever has not won the WSMVP since Mariano Rivera in 1999 and Ashby is not the team’s primary closer.
So I will go with Jacob Misiorowski throwing two elite starts in games one and five, as well as an impact relief appearance in game six.
I think these teams are pretty evenly matched – the Rays have the upper hand in starting pitching, the Brewers have the better bullpen. While the Brewers scored more runs in the regular season, the teams had similar rate stats (Milwaukee had a 105 OPS+, compared to Tampa Bay’s 103). The Rays’ starters have consistently worked deeper into games compared to Milwaukee, and I wonder at what point the wear and tear will start to get to the Brewers’ bullpen. The Rays don’t strike out often, which leads me to believe they can be the team that finally conquers Milwaukee’s relievers. Milwaukee’s offense was relentless against the Dodgers, so it won’t be easy for the Rays to keep the Brewers down.
Overall, I think this will be a hard-fought series, with the Rays emerging victorious in seven games. Drew Rasmussen will win World Series MVP, winning his starts in Game 1 and Game 5, then coming out of the bullpen to pitch in Game 7.
Brewers in 7, Jackson Chourio is MVP. I wish Bob Uecker was here to see it.
Brewers in six. This should be a really fun and competitive series between two teams who play baseball the right way. Pitching wins, especially in the postseason, so Jacob Misiorowski will win the MVP after authoring his postseason legacy with two elite starts and a gutsy appearance out of the bullpen with everything on the line.
Brewers in 6. Christian Yelich wins MVP as he lives up to his newly minted captain status. Tampa will give them a run for their money!
Rays in 7. Freddy Peralta World Series MVP, because why not. He enters in desperation relief to get the final out.

By STEVE MEGARGEE
MILWAUKEE (AP) — Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy was celebrating his team’s World Series appearance when he shared that recently crowned team captain Christian Yelich had predicted this moment several months before.
“Yeli said it early in the season,” Murphy said after the Brewers completed their NL Championship Series sweep of the Dodgers. “He said, ‘You’d better start believing because we’re going to the World Series,’ and we’re right here.”
There’s only one problem with this narrative. Yelich can’t recall making that proclamation.
“I don’t remember,” Yelich said Thursday, the day before the Brewers host the Tampa Bay Rays in their first World Series game since 1982. “He told me I said that. I don’t know. But I think throughout the year, you just believed that. I think you have to believe that and you have to expect to be here. You don’t want to approach it like, ‘Wow, I can’t believe we’re here.’ You should expect to be here, especially with the kind of team we’ve had.”
Whether Yelich actually said it or not, the fact his perceived comment would carry such weight comes as no surprise.
Yelich, 34, and pitcher Brandon Woodruff are the only players who have been on Milwaukee’s roster throughout the Brewers’ run of eight playoff appearances in nine seasons. The Brewers acquired him from Miami in 2018, and he was named NL MVP later that year. Yelich’s value in the clubhouse has remained as strong as ever, even as he’s battled injuries over the last several years and a drop in production this season.
Getting selected as Brewers’ first captain
Teammates say the Brewers’ decision to name Yelich the first team captain in franchise history on the final weekend of the regular season merely formalized what they already knew.
“He’s been a captain before he got the ‘C,’” outfielder Sal Frelick said. “We all know that.”
He’s one of three active captains in MLB, joining the New York Yankees’ Aaron Judge and the Kansas City Royals’ Salvador Perez.
Yelich’s appreciation for Brewers history was evident from the way he reacted to this honor. When the idea was proposed to Yelich, he initially wanted to make sure it was OK with Hall of Fame shortstop Robin Yount, who never had the captain title but is regarded as the best Brewers player ever.
Yount called Yelich’s concern “a very humbling” gesture that “certainly wasn’t necessary.”
“He certainly deserved that, earned that on his own,” Yount said. “The fact that the Brewers chose to actually give a captain’s ‘C’ on his jersey, and all of that. I think it’s great. I think the timing couldn’t have been better for something like this.”
Now Yelich is playing a major role in helping the Brewers get back to the World Series for the first time since Yount led them there during his MVP season of 1982. This hasn’t been a banner season for Yelich, whose .315 on-base percentage and .692 OPS were career lows.
Stepping up in postseason
But he has been coming through lately.
Yelich ended a string of 18 straight postseason games without an RBI when he singled home a run in Game 3 of the NL Division Series at San Diego. He has gone 7 for 24 at the plate this postseason, a .292 average that eclipses his regular-season average of .235.
Murphy says he noticed how much the “C” meant to Yelich.
“It was real for him,” Murphy said. “You can tell when you give someone something or you let somebody know something. It was real for Yelich, in a way that I was even shocked at. Since then, I don’t know the numbers, but I just know this guy is on point. He’s focused.
“He feels that responsibility. And I think it’s an easier responsibility for him to carry, because it’s so natural, than to try to carry the pressure of, ‘Hey, I’ve got to get four hits or I’ve got to do this.’ He’s way more important to this process than anyone knows.”
Yelich has been setting an example to his younger teammates for years.
“He took me under his wing my first big-league camp before I was even in the big leagues,” Frelick said. “Walking me through baserunning stuff. I’m like, ‘This guy has won an MVP. Why is he telling me how tight I have to cut the third-base bag when I’m running home from second?’ It’s because he just knows how to play the game. He cares. He knows that’s how to win baseball games. And he knows that if people hear it coming from him, they’ll then tell other guys how important it is.”
That kind of approach had Yelich and his younger teammates believing they could reach a World Series. Now they’re finally here.
“This is the expectation and the standard we wanted to set going into spring training,” Yelich said. “It isn’t like we woke up and found ourselves here. This was the goal and where we wanted to be.”

MILWAUKEE (AP) — The Miz will try to whiz his famous fastball by batters on baseball's biggest stage, opening a new-look World Series between teams guaranteed to produce a first-time champion.
Jacob Misiorowski brings his record-setting heat to the mound for the Milwaukee Brewers on Friday night when he throws the first pitch of the best-of-seven championship against the Tampa Bay Rays, a matchup of modest-money marvels who bumped off glamorous rivals with a throwback base-to-base style.
“Forrest Gump, everyone,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said Thursday, introducing his ace to the assembled media.
“I'm still fresh to all of this and I have no idea what the hell is going on,” Misiorowski said a few minutes later.
Few predicted this pairing of pennant winners when the season opened March 25. The first World Series with robot umpires is the first since 1980 between teams seeking their first championship and also could be the first with a 104 mph pitch — thanks to Misiorowski — and the first to be played totally indoors.
Milwaukee is in the Series for the second time after a 44-year absence — an appropriate number given that it was the jersey of the Cream City's most famous baseball player, Hank Aaron, who became a star with the Milwaukee Braves in the 1950s and ended his career with the expansion Brewers in the 1970s.
Both teams fell short in previous Series trips, the Brewers losing to St. Louis in 1982 and the Rays to Philadelphia in 2008 and to the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2020. Not since the Phillies beat Kansas City in 1980 have two teams met seeking their first title. The time before that was in 1920.
Rays players are excited to display their brand of baseball.
“We love watching those guys cause chaos,” Tampa Bay pitcher Steven Matz said of his team's bunters and speedsters. “Every time it’s first and third and someone lays down a bunt, we are just dying laughing in the bullpen.”
Misiorowski is likely to set a World Series velocity record
Misiorowski, a 24-year-old right-hander in his first full major league season, is a starting pitcher like no other. He threw 1,115 pitches of 100 mph or higher this year — shattering the old high of 673 since tracking began in 2008, by Jordan Hicks in 2018.
His fastest pitch was 105.5 mph to the Chicago Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 27, and he appears likely to break the 101.1 mph record for a Series starter by the New York Mets' Noah Syndergaard in 2015 and possibly the overall Series high of 103.2 mph by Cubs reliever Aroldis Chapman to Cleveland's Coco Crisp in Game 2 of 2016.
Misiorowski didn't finish the fifth inning in either of his first two postseason starts this year. Batters have swung at 94 of his 182 postseason pitches and fouled off 51 — 28% of pitches and 54% of swings.
“He hasn’t been as crisp,” Murphy said. “They’re obviously looking at an area. They’re trying to exploit everything. He’s exposed, like all these guys get at some point.”
Martinez a surprise starter for Rays
Nick Martinez will start for Tampa Bay, which gives extra rest to Drew Rasmussen ahead of Game 2 and Freddy Peralta before Game 3.
A 36-year-old right-hander with his fourth major league team, Martinez took the Rays to dinner Wednesday at Carnevor, a top Milwaukee steakhouse. He invites teammates, who have nicknamed him “El Presidente,” to a restaurant in every road city.
“To when I first got to the league, I’ve been around guys that knew how to control a clubhouse and for lack of a better term, knew how to throw a party,” Martinez said. “Getting the guys together is important. Creating that off-the-field chemistry translates to on the field.”
Brewers and Rays have throwback offenses
In an age where power bats usually rule, Milwaukee scored a major league-low 32.1% of its runs on homers and Tampa Bay was second-lowest at 34.4%, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
Brewers captain Christian Yelich says “we’ve done a good job of being kind of chameleons.”
“It's cool that you don't have to be the team to hit 170 home runs a game or whatever,” Misiorowski said. “You can win a baseball game so many different ways.”
Rays batters had the fewest strikeouts among the 30 teams and Tampa Bay’s 45 sacrifice bunts were the most among American League teams since 2015.
“If we had a club that was built with a bunch of boppers, we probably wouldn’t be bunting and stealing bases,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “I think we already have made bunting cool.”
After back-to-back Dodgers titles, MLB will have a small-payroll champion
This marks the first time since 1991 that both Series teams are in the bottom half of payrolls: the Brewers were 19th as of Aug. 31 and the Rays 25th. Milwaukee, MLB's smallest market, could become the first small-market champion since Kansas City in 2015. The Rays rank 15th in market size.
To reach the Series, the Brewers swept the deep-pocketed, two-time champion Dodgers in the NL Championship Series and the Rays swept the New York Yankees in an AL Division Series.
Yelich, the highest-paid player in the Series, was 44th overall in the majors on opening day. Yandy Díaz, who earns most among the Rays, ranked 154th.
Robot umps are changing games
Batters have succeeded on 63% of challenges during the postseason in the first year of the Automated Ball-Strike System, winning 40 of 63 appeals to the robot umps. That is up from 49% during the regular season.
Catchers' 58% success rate in the playoffs (58 of 99) is down a tick from 59% during the regular season and pitchers are 1 for 1 — Tampa Bay’s Griffin Jax made the only challenge. The 60% overall rate is up from 54% in the regular season.
Tampa Bay's batters have yet to make a postseason challenge. Milwaukee's have won 4 of 7, including a perfect 2 for 2 by Jake Bauers.
Brewers catcher William Contreras has won 60% (12 of 20) and Rays catcher Liam Hicks 67% (8 of 12).
Rest vs. rust: Extra time off hasn't been helpful in recent years
Milwaukee will have had seven days off going into the opener.
While teams with less rest are 15-15 in the Series since Wild Card Era started in 1995, they are 12-4 since 2009.
___
Ronald Blum, The Associated Press

Welcome to a most fantastically interesting World Series, in which focusing on the size of the markets involved completely misses the forest for the trees. It’s a No. 1-vs.-No. 1 matchup, just the sixth time in the past 30 years that’s happened. It’s a pair of fanbases who have never won before, which marks the first time since 1980 (Royals vs. Phillies) that’s happened, and thus only the second time in more than a century, since the previous time had been 1920.
It’s a matchup of teams that have more than a few connections. Note that Tampa Bay’s top two starters, Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta, each came up with Milwaukee, and were teammates on the 2020-21 Brewers. Note, also, that NLCS MVP Jake Bauers made his debut with Tampa Bay back in 2018, and that Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold spent nine years in the Tampa Bay front office before moving to Wisconsin.
It's more than just that. Depending on how you view your baseball aesthetics, it's a delightfully throwback sort of on-field style. It’s not that these teams eschew analytical thinking -- exactly the opposite, really -- but no team struck out less than the Rays, each team finished in the top five in steals and the bottom 10 in homers, and the bunt hits leaderboard goes “Tampa Bay first, Milwaukee second.”
Throw in a pair of excellent defenses, and you know what you’re going to get here, which is excellent baseball played by a pair of teams that actually look a whole lot like one another. We know what else we're going to get, too: an incredibly interesting series. Which side has the edge?
Catcher
William Contreras, over the past five years, has a pretty solid argument to make as being the best all-around catcher in the National League. While his bat over the last two seasons (110 OPS+) isn’t quite what it was at his peak from 2022-24 (129 OPS+), it’s reliably solid, and then of course he’s been fantastic in eight playoff games, posting a 1.157 OPS with three homers. It’s hard to overstate how important the midseason acquisition of Liam Hicks (129 OPS+ in 41 games for Tampa Bay) was, really helping to lengthen a top-heavy lineup, though he hasn’t done much with the bat in the playoffs. Given relatively similar defensive value, we’ll give a small edge based on track record.
Advantage: Brewers
First base
It's a tale of two winding paths here, as Jonathan Aranda finally had his breakout last season, a decade after he signed as an amateur free agent with Tampa Bay, and of course Jake Bauers' long road to get to this point has been well-chronicled. Bauers has the offensive edge both in terms of power and getting on base, and neither are terribly strong defensive players, so given the mild 2026 regular-season advantage and also the superior performance in October, it’s hard not to choose Bauers on this. Great stories, both.
Advantage: Brewers
Second base
Brice Turang is the best all-around second baseman in the game, pairing excellent defense with a more recently found power stroke, popping 21 homers and driving in 100. The Rays have certainly found some ways to get value out of their second-base duo of Richie Palacios and Ben Williamson, but it’s a relatively below-average spot for Tampa Bay and, either way, we’re comparing to Milwaukee’s best-in-class superstar. This one is probably the biggest mismatch of any pairing on the list.
Advantage: Brewers
Shortstop
Here’s how you know how well-regarded Taylor Walls is on defense: The Rays continue to play him every day despite a near-total lack of offense from the position, as he’s posted all of a .381 OPS this month, and even that was juiced a little by the inexplicable three walks that Cleveland issued him in ALCS Game 6. It’s not just a small-sample thing, either, as Walls has been a routinely ineffective hitter for the entirety of his career.
There’s no doubt that Milwaukee’s Cooper Pratt is a stronger offensive force, though that’s been more good than great, with a league-average line as a rookie and a mostly singles-based approach in the playoffs. While he’s expected to be a quality shortstop as his career progresses, a number of important miscues in the postseason tilt this one to the more surehanded Walls.
Advantage: Rays
Third base
If there’s some argument that this series features more depth than true superstars, then that case falls apart a little at third, where Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero posted his second consecutive 40-plus homer season on his way to, most likely, some high placement on AL MVP ballots. It’s true that prior to his ALCS Game 6 homer, his bat had been relatively quiet in October, but we’re also talking about all of eight games against some of the best pitching the sport has to offer. (The average fastball he’s seen? 96.8 mph.) There’s an obvious speed-and-defense edge for Milwaukee in David Hamilton and Joey Ortiz, but not quite so much that you’d take either or both over Caminero, or that it’s really close at all.
Advantage: Rays
Left field
This is actually the most fun comparison, because who do you like more, the 22-year-old power-and-defense superstar in Jackson Chourio -- the only player in history to have three 20-20 seasons through age-22 -- or the 25-year-old elite speed-and-contact guy in Chandler Simpson, who improved his defense to the point that both were named Gold Glove finalists last week? It’s yet another reminder that there’s more than one way to provide value, and certainly both teams are very pleased with their situations here. It’s hard, though, not to default to Chourio, who might already be a top-20 position player in the sport. If both can run and field, and only one has any power, then the advantage writes itself.
Advantage: Brewers
Center field
In Garrett Mitchell and Jonny DeLuca, you have two very strong defensive center fielders, though you’d probably give the slight edge here to DeLuca. (Cedric Mullins also carries a good glove, though this spot has belonged to DeLuca all month.) The question about their bats is what shape of production you prefer, in that Mitchell struck out considerably more than DeLuca, but he also had an on-base percentage 54 points higher, thanks in large part to a walk rate three times as high. While we’re not weighing postseason performance too much here, it’s worth noting that Mitchell has had some huge hits, while DeLuca mostly has not. This is about as razor-thin as we’ll see here, but even if Mitchell’s glove isn’t as good, it’s still good, and he gets on base. Edge, Milwaukee. A small one, anyway.
Advantage: Brewers
Right field
For everything that Sal Frelick has done for the Brewers over his four seasons with the team -- and he has done quite a bit -- this was not a terribly strong season for him, posting a career-worst 70 OPS+, and he’s managed only three singles and a few walks in the playoffs. That’s not to say that he can’t help the team win in other ways, because he can and does, but Tampa Bay’s Victor Mesa Jr. has been one of the team’s breakout stars, putting up not only a 127 OPS+ but also some truly elite defensive metrics, in just half a season. You’re already familiar, anyway, with his absolute cannon of a throwing arm. Mesa Jr. wasn’t on the Opening Day roster and didn’t even join the Rays for good until late May. He might just be one of the most important players in the World Series, though.
Advantage: Rays
Designated hitter
It would be hard to find two players who mean more to their respective teams than veterans Yandy Díaz (in his eighth season with Tampa Bay) and recently appointed Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich (in his ninth season as a Brewer). Neither plays the field much anymore, nor is either at or near their peak of offensive performance these days. But Díaz far outperformed Yelich during the regular season (124 OPS+ to 91 OPS+, where again, 100 is average), and that’s held true in the postseason, too, where Yelich has been held out of certain games against tough lefties in favor of Andrew Vaughn. At DH, literally the only thing that matters is “dangerous bat,” and that’s Díaz still, after all these years.
Advantage: Rays
Starting pitchers
If we’re talking about each team’s top three starters, which represent the bulk of a postseason rotation, then it’s Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and Robert Gasser for Milwaukee, and Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta and Nick Martinez for Tampa Bay. Those six pitchers, so far in the playoffs, have combined for a 1.87 ERA. They’re not that good, obviously, with every underlying metric saying that the strikeout rate has been just average, and that they’ve been bailed out to some extent by excellent defense and relief pitching.
Still: When Misiorowski -- the presumptive NL Cy Young winner, the most dominant per-batter pitcher of the moment -- has the highest postseason ERA of these six, you know how strong each team is here. You really can’t look at full-season stats, either, because it goes without saying that the Tampa Bay version of Peralta is a very different pitcher than New York version we saw prior to the Trade Deadline. Misiorowski is the best of the six, but is he that much better than Rasmussen right now, himself an ace? Maybe not.
These are two strengths, but we like Tampa Bay ever so slightly more for one reason: depth. No Milwaukee starter, not even the top ones, has managed to get past five innings in the playoffs so far, which puts a lot of pressure on the bullpens. (There’s a particularly interesting angle here if Tampa Bay’s high-contact, flat-swing hitters can foul off enough Misiorowski pitches to wear him out, as has already happened to him this month.) If you look past the top three, you’d probably take Tampa Bay’s Griffin Jax and Ian Seymour to get outs a little more than Milwaukee’s Shane Drohan and Dustin May.
They’re both good, obviously. They’re World Series starting rotations. We’d give the ever-so-slight edge to Tampa Bay in a best of seven.
Advantage: Rays
Relief pitchers
If Milwaukee’s starters have been more good than great this month, then their relievers have more than picked up the slack, as you’ve almost certainly heard the note that in 40 2/3 postseason innings, the Brewers' bullpen has allowed all of six earned runs. While most of the focus there lands on Aaron Ashby or closer Trevor Megill, realize that JoJo Romero has a 47% strikeout rate this month, and that Abner Uribe, Antonio Senzatela, Megill and Ashby are all averaging more than 98 mph on their heaters this month. In fact, it is the second-hardest-throwing bullpen of the pitch tracking era (since 2008) -- at 98 mph even -- and the hardest that doesn’t include Mason Miller.
It makes, then, for an ironic matchup against a Tampa Bay bullpen that is A) also very good but B) does not throw hard, comparatively, at just 93.2 mph. (That goes down slightly, if you don't include Peralta’s impressive appearance in ALCS Game 4.) Much depends on the status of Bryan Baker, their All-Star closer, who was used so heavily against Cleveland that his fastball, which averaged 96.3 mph during the regular season, sunk below 93 mph in ALCS Game 6.
He was still good, of course. All the Rays are. It’s just hard not to go with Milwaukee, given their superior depth and full rest.
Advantage: Brewers
Prediction
It should be clear by now that this is an incredibly tightly matched series between two mirror-image teams, the best in their respective leagues, and you could as easily claim “rust or rest” for Milwaukee after their layoff, no matter which narrative you’d like to go with. Milwaukee has the biggest-name pitcher in Misiorowski; Tampa Bay has clearly the biggest star hitter in Caminero; and both sides play strong defense and win in ways that aren’t just waiting for the homer.
We like that Milwaukee has the home-field advantage, and the bullpen edge, and also that their lineup just seems a little deeper; in the second half of the season, no team -- not the Dodgers, not the Cubs, not anyone -- got more production from the No. 6 through 9 spots in their lineup than Milwaukee. That’s in part because of the middle infield, where the Brewers were third best, while Tampa Bay was third weakest. There’s at least some question about what shape Baker will be in, though three days of rest before the World Series ought to help.
It won’t be a cakewalk, because there’s too much talent and similarity on both sides for that. But every small edge matters, and Milwaukee has enough of them that we expect the second World Series title in city history, and the first for the Brewers franchise. Get ready to slide, Bernie.
Brewers in seven.

The Milwaukee Brewers' World Series roster should look almost exactly the same as it has so far this postseason.
Fresh off a dominant sweep in the NLCS against the back-to-back World Series champion Dodgers, the Brewers had a full week to prepare for this winner-take-all best-of-seven series.
Looking at the Rays lineup and how they construct things, it'll be interesting to see what Murphy goes with in the upcoming series.
Remember, Milwaukee has a pair of pitchers who have yet to pitch in the postseason despite being on the roster the entire time.
If there was ever a time for Big Woo to come back, it would be now, though the team must carefully weigh all of its options before pulling the trigger.

Brewers make one roster change
When it comes to William Contreras and Gary Sanchez, neither of those players is going anywhere. Sanchez has yet to catch in the playoffs, and he likely won't, but he had a huge pinch-hit walk against Mason Miller in Game 2 of the NLDS.
Milwaukee will still carry six infielders and five outfielders. There isn't a world where they should mess with any of those 11 players. There are no injuries that have been made available to the public, and there's no one else who could fill those spots at this point in the year.
Pitching-wise, Chad Patrick has gotten loose a few times, so that's the only thing keeping him on the roster.
Woodruff shouldn't start a game unless it's at home and he's used as an opener. But, with where he's at, it certainly feels like he could give this team some useful bullpen innings, and there's no one more deserving to be on the roster than him.

item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays — the top team in the American League — has held its own to achieve the third pennant in franchise history, and their second this decade.
The Milwaukee Brewers are back in the World Series for the first time since 1982, and they're doing it as the National League's best team. The 103-win Crew swept the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS and now host the Tampa Bay Rays in a matchup of two franchise-first title seekers. Game 1 is Friday at American Family Field.
Here's a position-by-position look at the Brewers as they prepare for the Rays.
Catcher
William Contreras is the lead backstop for Milwaukee, and one of the most popular Brewers, as he has been one of the more reliable all-around catchers in the National League in recent years and in the playoffs, as his bat has stayed productive into October. He posted a strong 1.157 OPS with three homers through the NLCS while handling a staff that mixes elite velocity with a deep lefty presence.
At backup, the more familiar Gary Sánchez provides a power-oriented option off the bench.
Infield
The Brewers' infield blends elite defense, speed, and opportunistic offense.
- First base: Jake Bauers. The NLCS MVP has been the postseason story for Milwaukee. A well-known Rays prospect if you've read this site for any length of time, Bauers nearly retired but returned for what he considered one more season last year to keep his health insurance benefits after his wife became pregnant with their second child. Fast forward two seasons, and he has delivered lengthy at bats with power and timely hitting throughout October while providing solid enough defense at the corner. Veteran White Sox infielder Andrew Vaughn has also seen time at first and as a right-handed bat off the bench or at DH against lefties.
- Second base: Brice Turang. One of the best all-around second basemen in baseball and the No. 2 hitter. Turang combines Gold Glove-caliber defense with improved power (21 home runs and 100 RBIs in the regular season) and baserunning. He's a clear mismatch advantage and not to be trifled with.
- Shortstop: Cooper Pratt. The 22-year old rookie shortstop has started the bulk of the postseason games. He's shown a contact-oriented approach and improving glove work as the year has progressed, and pushing the previous starter Ortiz into a third base platoon.
- Third base: Joey Ortiz / David Hamilton. This has been a platoon/mix-and-match spot. The right handed hitting Ortiz and left handed hitting Hamilton now split time depending on matchups. If we are drawing comparisons, neither matches Junior Caminero's power, but both offer speed and defensive flexibility that fits Milwaukee's style.
Outfield
Milwaukee's outfield is built on athleticism, defense, and a rising star.
- Left field: Jackson Chourio. This 22-year-old superstar has continued his rapid ascent in 2026. Already with multiple 20-20 seasons under his belt, Chourio brings power, speed, and improving defense. He's the dynamic centerpiece of the lineup, their version of a Junior Caminero, and fun to watch.
- Center field: Garrett Mitchell. Strong defensive center fielder who has delivered several big hits in the playoffs, including a go-ahead home run in the NLCS clincher. He gets on base and covers ground.
- Right field: Sal Frelick. Elite defender with speed and contact skills. Luis Lara has spelled him against left-handers and provides another athletic option. The group ranks among the best defensive outfields in the league.
Technically also an outfielder, the Designated Hitter, Christian Yelich, remains in the lineup and was recently named club captain. While not at his peak production levels, his experience and ability to still impact games remain valuable, especially against right-handed pitching.
Rotation
Manager Pat Murphy has utilized short leashes and heavy bullpen support, but has a solid rotation heading into the World Series:
- Jacob Misiorowski — The clear ace and yet to be crowned NL Cy Young winner (16-5, 1.80 ERA, 252 strikeouts in the regular season). He's started Game 1 of both the NLDS and NLCS and will surely open the World Series. To say his high-velocity stuff that ranks among the best is an understatement. I half expected Misiorowski to mean fast in Polish, but apparently it's something closer to bear.
- Logan Henderson — The reliable No. 2. Solid second-half performer who has handled Game 2 duties effectively in his sophomore season as a homegrown talent.
- Robert Gasser — Emerged as the preferred Game 3 option after strong late-season form and solid postseason outings (including shutout work in the NLCS). He was acquired in the Josh Hader trade with San Diego, over came a UCL surgery in 2025, and started the year in Triple-A, making his rise a bit unexpected. His dad's best friend is evidently Vin Diesel.
- Dustin May (with Shane Drohan as an Opener) — May has postseason experience but has been used carefully; Florida State alumni Drohan opened Game 4 in the NLCS, and the southpaw seems likely to get the nod again given how well that went last time.
No starter has gone particularly deep in October, which is by design. Milwaukee trusts its relievers to take over after four or five innings, limiting any time-through-the-order penalties.
Bullpen
This unit has been the difference-maker. The Brewers' bullpen allowed just six earned runs across more than 40 postseason innings heading into the World Series and featured relievers earning the win in all four NLCS games during the sweep of Los Angeles.
- Trevor Megill — 6'8" Closer. Reliable late-inning presence, and a bit of an invention by the Brewers, having been added for a PTBNL in April 2023.
- Abner Uribe — Primary setup man. High-velocity right-hander who has been outstanding, despite blowing a save in Game 3 of the NLCS he's been their best bullpen arm this month.
- Aaron Ashby — Left-handed workhorse who has been nearly unhittable in October (multiple scoreless multi-inning outings) and got the save in Game 4 of the sweep.
- DL Hall / JoJo Romero — Additional lefty depth options that each were credited wins in the NLCS.
Regular season starter Kyle Harrison will likely find his way into the mix as well. The group throws exceptionally hard on average and enters the series fully rested after the NLCS sweep and the Rays' longer ALCS.
Conclusion
The Brewers' formula is clear: elite defense, contact and speed on offense, an electric frontline starter, and a lights-out bullpen that can cover the middle and late innings.
Against a similarly constructed Rays team that also emphasizes pitching, defense, and small-ball elements, the series should be tight, low-scoring, and decided by the margins. Milwaukee holds home-field advantage and the deeper, harder-throwing relief corps—two factors that could prove decisive in a first-time-champion showdown.

The Milwaukee Brewers have been the definition of sustained success over the last nine years, reaching the postseason eight times, but after a sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers, they have finally reached the World Series.
Milwaukee has won its division in each of the past four seasons and six times in total over the last nine years, but despite its consistent talent, it has not reached the World Series until now. The Brewers have been dominant for nearly a decade, a stretch that coincides with the arrival of superstar Christian Yelich.
Yelich, 34, quickly became the face of the Brewers organization after winning the National League MVP award in 2018, and he nearly did it again the next season. Though Yelich may not be the same player he used to be, he still has made such an impact that Milwaukee named him the team's first official captain in September. He joins Aaron Judge and Salvador Perez as the only active MLB captains.
Yelich has been the face of the Brewers' franchise for years
"Christian Yelich joined the Milwaukee Brewers following a 2017 trade and quickly became the face of the franchise," Bleacher Report's Erik Beaston wrote on Tuesday. "He won the NL MVP award in 2018 and earned 'captain' status with the organization as its leader, both in front of the cameras and behind the scenes. He has been through the highs and the lows with the team, and while he may not be quite the player he once was, there is no denying that he is as synonymous with this generation of the Milwaukee squad as anyone.
"After a season that saw him deliver 104 hits, 12 home runs, 59 RBI, and a slash line of .235/.315/.378, it will bear watching as to whether or not Yelich still has that superstar magic left in him and can help propel his organization to its first world championship. A close friend of the late Brewers play-by-play announcer, the legendary Bob Uecker, Yelich figures to be playing for teammates both here and gone when he takes to the diamond Friday night at American Family Field."
Yelich has stepped up throughout the postseason, slashing .292/.370/.333 with three RBIs, two walks and three runs scored. After years of leading the Brewers, the 34-year-old is finally getting the chance to play on the biggest stage and potentially help Milwaukee win its first World Series.
Game 1 of the World Series is set for Friday, and Yelich will need to maintain his high level of play if the Brewers want to take down the Tampa Bay Rays.
Shaun McAvoy is a freelance writer with experience working with Newsweek, NESN, The Sporting News and SportsNet Pittsburgh. Shaun is a Boston-area native, growing up in Billerica, Massachusetts, and graduating from Merrimack College with a degree in Sports Management and Communications and Media. Shaun is a massive Star Wars, Marvel and DC fan.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- Jake Bauers put his team’s determination on full display, getting the Milwaukee Brewers within one victory of their first World Series appearance in 44 years.
Bauers turned an 11-pitch at-bat into a go-ahead two-run homer in the seventh inning as the Brewers took a commanding 3-0 lead in the National League Championship Series with a 6-2 victory Wednesday night against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Milwaukee will aim for a sweep of the best-of-7 series tonight at Dodger Stadium.
Garrett Mitchell followed Bauers with a homer of his own as the Southern California natives put on a show in front of family and friends in a ballpark where the home team has played the bully for more than a decade.
“We play for each other. It’s as simple as that, man,” Bauers said. “Any time there’s a mistake, an error, a walk, pitchers give up runs, hitters strike out in a big spot, the only thing anybody’s thinking about is how can I help pick that guy up? How can I help pick that guy up and do my part to win this game?”
Rookie left-hander Robert Gasser gave up three hits over five scoreless innings as the Brewers moved closer to the franchise’s second trip to the World Series. The Brewers made their lone Fall Classic appearance in 1982 as an American League team, losing in seven games to the St. Louis Cardinals.
Jackson Chourio led off the game with a first-pitch homer off Dodgers left-hander Blake Snell as Milwaukee showed its power capabilities after finishing last in the National League in homers during the regular season with 154.
“Job’s not finished yet,” Mitchell said. “Just got to take it a day at a time, not really worried about what’s happened today, what happened yesterday or what’s coming tomorrow. We’ve just got to show up and continue to play our brand of baseball and continue doing it for one another.”
Will Smith hit a two-run double for the Dodgers, who won the past two World Series titles. Los Angeles is trying to become the first National League club to win three consecutive Fall Classic championships.
Los Angeles manager Dave Roberts moved Shohei Ohtani to sixth in the batting order with the superstar in a postseason slump. Ohtani went 1-for-2 with a walk and a hit-by-pitch. The Dodgers’ offense was held to five hits in Game 3 after collecting three in Game 2.
“I haven’t digested this one,” Roberts said when asked about potential lineup changes for Game 4. “They’re going to run a bullpen game. Just trying to figure out which guys we want to be in there, how you kind of construct the lineup, but I haven’t thought about that one yet.”
Snell appeared to recover from Chourio’s ambush home run before he was rocked by consecutive home runs with no outs in the seventh. Snell (0-1) allowed four runs on four hits in six-plus innings with two walks and nine strikeouts.
“I just left the fastball over the middle to Bauers,” said Snell, who was in the Tampa Bay Rays organization with Bauers from 2015-18. “… I’ve seen the ups and downs he’s been through, and it’s been a lot of downs. So for him to go through this right now, he’s earned it. Hats off to him. What an at-bat.”
Trailing 1-0 from the jump, the Dodgers managed to put their leadoff batter on base in four of the first six innings before finally breaking through.
Gasser was replaced by right-hander Abner Uribe to open the sixth inning, and the reliever walked three of the first four batters he faced to load the bases, including a walk to Ohtani. Smith delivered a double off the wall in left-center field for a 2-1 lead after entering the game in a 1-for-25 slump.
Los Angeles failed to add onto the lead in the inning against left-hander DL Hall (3-0) when Enrique Hernandez and Tommy Edman struck out to end the threat.
Milwaukee responded immediately when Andrew Vaughn walked to open the seventh before Bauers’ epic at-bat. Two pitches later, Mitchell went over the wall in right-center field for a 4-2 advantage to end Snell’s outing.
Bauers had a similar plate appearance in Game 2 when he worked a 12-pitch walk with two outs in the third inning and Christian Yelich followed with a two-run single.
“Yeah, there was for sure a moment where I thought to myself like, ‘Oh, you’re in it again,’” Bauers said. “As far as the approach for the at-bat, I didn’t want to miss a fastball.”
The Brewers added to their lead in the eighth when Brice Turang scored on a Justin Wrobleski wild pitch, and Joey Ortiz tacked on an RBI single in the ninth.
Hall threw 2⅓ scoreless innings. Brewers closer Trevor Megill got the last four outs, striking out the final two batters, for his fourth save of the postseason.

item.content:encoded:
William Contreras se consolida como el mejor bate latino de los playoffs y acerca a Milwaukee a una barrida sobre los Dodgers.
William Contreras llegó a esta postemporada como una de las piezas centrales de los Milwaukee Brewers, pero su producción está superando incluso las previsiones más optimistas. El receptor venezolano respondió en los turnos de mayor presión y se convirtió en el bate latino más productivo de estos playoffs, con una combinación de contacto, poder y capacidad para impulsar carreras.
Su actuación más reciente confirmó ese momento. Contreras conectó un jonrón de 436 pies en el quinto inning del segundo juego de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional y empató la pizarra 4-4 ante los Dodgers. Una entrada después, pegó el sencillo que produjo la carrera de la ventaja definitiva en la victoria 7-4 de Milwaukee.
Ese resultado permitió que los Brewers pusieran 2-0 la serie antes del viaje a Los Ángeles. Contreras terminó el encuentro con tres hits en cuatro turnos, tres carreras impulsadas y una base por bolas. Cada uno de sus imparables produjo el empate o puso a Milwaukee adelante.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Pagés, Chourio, Contreras y Díaz: cuatro historias rumbo a la Serie Mundial
¿Qué números tiene William Contreras en estos playoffs?
El venezolano registra promedio de .391, tres jonrones, cinco carreras impulsadas y cuatro anotadas en 23 turnos al bate. También suma nueve hits, cuatro boletos, porcentaje de embasado de .481, slugging de .783 y OPS de 1.264 durante seis partidos.
Su promedio lo ubica en el cuarto lugar entre todos los bateadores de MLB en esta postemporada. Los tres jugadores que aparecen por encima son Nico Hoerner, Ben Rice y Michael Harris II, por lo cual Contreras ocupa el primer puesto entre los peloteros latinoamericanos.
La cifra también refleja un salto importante frente a su rendimiento durante la campaña regular. Contreras cerró esa etapa con promedio de .270, 18 cuadrangulares y 94 impulsadas en 147 juegos. En octubre elevó su promedio 121 puntos y mantuvo una producción de poder mucho más alta en un momento decisivo de la temporada.
Ese contraste explica por qué su desempeño supera lo que podía anticiparse a partir de sus números de temporada. El catcher no solo acumula hits. También los consigue en situaciones que modifican el rumbo de los partidos.
¿Por qué Contreras es el mejor bate de Milwaukee?
Contreras lidera a los bateadores regulares de Milwaukee en promedio, jonrones y OPS durante esta postemporada. Sus tres cuadrangulares representan el 60% de los cinco que acumula el equipo, mientras su promedio de .391 supera el .368 de Christian Yelich.
Los números adquieren más valor por su puesto. El venezolano cumple las exigencias defensivas de la receptoría y mantiene presencia constante en el corazón del lineup. Durante la temporada regular lideró a los catchers de las Grandes Ligas en entradas detrás del plato y fijó una marca de la franquicia con 89 carreras impulsadas mientras actuó como receptor.
Milwaukee también necesita su capacidad para alargar turnos. Contreras solo suma tres ponches en 27 apariciones al plato y recibió cuatro boletos. Ese control de la zona le permite alcanzar una base con frecuencia y evita que los lanzadores rivales encuentren salidas sencillas en la parte fuerte del orden ofensivo.
Contreras es ahora mismo el mejor bate de los Brewers porque combina promedio, poder y producción en momentos clave. Su impacto no depende de una sola actuación. El venezolano ya conectó tres jonrones y alcanzó base en 13 de sus 27 visitas al plato.
¿Qué necesita Milwaukee para barrer a los Dodgers?
La serie regresará a Los Ángeles con los Brewers a dos victorias del título de la Liga Nacional. Milwaukee tendrá la oportunidad de completar la barrida si gana los próximos dos encuentros en Dodger Stadium.
El cambio de sede aumentará la exigencia para una alineación que hasta ahora encontró respuestas oportunas. Los Dodgers cuentan con profundidad en su cuerpo de lanzadores y tendrán el respaldo de su público, pero llegan al tercer juego después de perder los dos primeros choques de la serie.
Milwaukee necesita que Contreras conserve su disciplina y su capacidad para castigar lanzamientos en la zona. Su bate puede marcar la diferencia frente a un rival que no ofrece mucho margen, en especial si los juegos vuelven a llegar cerrados a los innings finales.
Los Brewers también requerirán apoyo del resto de la ofensiva y en este escenario ChristianYelich (.368) luce como otro nombre clave pues el bateador designado batea por encima de .300. Si el venezolano mantiene este nivel, Milwaukee contará con una opción real de barrer a los Dodgers en California y asegurar su boleto a la Serie Mundial.

Los Milwaukee Brewers aprovecharon los errores y las oportunidades ofensivas para vencer 7-4 a Los Angeles Dodgers en el segundo juego de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional. Con 12 imparables, los locales remontaron en distintos momentos del encuentro y tomaron una ventaja de 2-0 en la serie.
Vinny Castilla elogia a Jonathan Aranda por su actuación con Tampa Bay en los playoffs de MLB
El conjunto angelino llegó a ponerse al frente en tres ocasiones, pero no consiguió contener la respuesta de Milwaukee. Los Dodgers encontraron carreras en la primera, tercera y quinta entradas; sin embargo, los Brewers respondieron con batazos oportunos para cambiar el partido.
William Contreras y Brice Turang lideraron el ataque de Milwaukee
William Contreras fue una de las grandes figuras de la tarde al terminar con tres imparables y tres carreras impulsadas, incluido un cuadrangular en la quinta entrada. El receptor conectó también sencillos productores en el primer y sexto episodios para mantener a su equipo en la pelea.
Brice Turang también tuvo una actuación determinante, con tres carreras anotadas y una impulsada. Christian Yelich produjo dos carreras con un sencillo en la tercera entrada, mientras Jake Bauers contribuyó con un imparable productor en el octavo episodio para ampliar la ventaja de los Brewers
JoJo Romero se queda con la victoria; Brock Stewart carga con la derrota
El mexicano-estadounidense JoJo Romero se acreditó la victoria, mientras que Brock Stewart fue el pitcher derrotado y Aaron Ashby consiguió el salvamento. Milwaukee encontró la manera de inclinar el encuentro a su favor y cerró la novena entrada sin permitir una reacción de los Dodgers.
Los Brewers aseguraron el triunfo con dos carreras en la octava entrada, cuando Turang conectó un sencillo productor y Bauers agregó otro imparable que permitió anotar una carrera más.
Ahora, la serie se trasladará a Los Ángeles para el tercer encuentro, programado para el miércoles 14 de octubre, donde los Dodgers estarán obligados a reaccionar si quieren mantenerse con vida en la pelea por el campeonato de la Liga Nacional.

item.content:encoded:
The National League’s two best teams in the regular season are the last two standing at the end. The 103-win Brewers against the 100-win Dodgers.
Who’s ready for a rematch of last year’s NLCS?
“Coming into the postseason, you had a feeling you were going to have to go through L.A.,” said Brewers designated hitter Christian Yelich. “They’re back-to-back champs, and they’re a great team. We have a lot of respect for those guys.
“At the same time, we feel like we can play with anybody when we play our game. When we play our brand of baseball, when we play clean and execute, we’re a really hard team to beat. We’re going to go in there and grind.”
For the Dodgers, this year’s NLCS is a chance to continue a bid for a third consecutive World Series title.
For the Brewers, it’s a chance at redemption. They have been to the League Championship Series five times in their franchise history, and this is the third in a row that pits them against the Dodgers. They lost a seven-game thriller in 2018, then got swept in four games last year, when Brewers hitters were shut down by the Dodgers’ superstar starting pitchers.
Will this year be different?
"In this sport, you can't carry previous postseasons into this postseason. Everything is a new chapter," said Dodgers utility man Kiké Hernández. "Every time you take the field in October, you get an opportunity to rewrite your story."
When is the game and how can I watch it?
Game 1 is underway at American Family Field and airing nationally on FOX, FOX Deportes and FOX One.
All series are available in the US on MLB.TV with authentication to a participating Pay TV provider. Games also are available live internationally, although not in Canada. Sportsnet is MLB's exclusive English language broadcaster in Canada for every Postseason game, while TVA Sports will be covering the entire AL Postseason and the World Series in French and Broadcaster RDS will cover the entire NL Postseason in French.
Skubal showed exactly why the Dodgers swung big to acquire him from the Tigers ahead of the Trade Deadline in his NLDS Game 1 start, when he struck out seven across six innings of one-run ball against the Braves. Now, he will take the hill as L.A. begins the next stage of its title defense.
Misiorowski’s first pitch of NLDS Game 1 was 104.8 mph, the fastest postseason pitch in the pitch tracking era, which dates back to 2008. But the Padres made him work, fouling off an incredible 30 pitches in the first four innings to knock Misiorowski out of the game by the fifth at 88 pitches. He was in the bullpen for Game 4 in San Diego, and even warmed up in the ninth, but was not needed, meaning he will be rested and ready for the Dodgers. In three career appearances against L.A. – two starts in the regular season and one relief outing in last year’s NLCS – Misiorowski has a 1.59 ERA and 27 strikeouts vs. three walks in 17 innings.
What are the starting lineups?
Dodgers: The Dodgers have dropped Shohei Ohtani in the lineup as his struggles from the end of the regular season have bled into the beginning of the postseason. Misiorowski has been tough on L.A. in the past, so manager Dave Roberts shuffled his lineup to optimize the matchups.
Brewers: The Brewers don’t hit many home runs, but they can hit home runs, and they can score in a lot of ways. During the regular season, they were second in the Majors in runs scored by hitting for average (.258, first in MLB), getting on base (.341, first), stealing bases (152, fifth), bunting (32 bunt hits, second) and generally refusing to swing the bat until they wanted to (lowest swing percentage in MLB and lowest chase percentage). Against the Padres in the NLDS, they came from behind in two of the three victories. Here’s how they're lining up against Skubal in Game 1.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Dodgers: Edwin Díaz saved the final two games of the NLDS and is firmly back in the closer's mix, with Tanner Scott also an option to lock down save situations. The Dodgers added a 13th pitcher while setting their 26-man roster for the NL Championship Series. Left-hander Justin Wrobleski joined the bullpen, while speed option Hyeseong Kim was left off the roster.
Brewers: Brewers relievers covered 19 innings in four games against the Padres with a 0.47 ERA and a .169 opposing average, led by the late-inning trio of left-hander Aaron Ashby, right-hander Abner Uribe and righty closer Trevor Megill. Uribe pitched in all four games, and Ashby and Megill in three, so a couple days off will be appreciated.
Any injuries of note?
Dodgers: Ohtani (right biceps, left knee) and Freeman (right knee) are managing lingering injuries. Rojas exited Game 3 with lower back pain, and while his availability for the beginning of the NLCS was uncertain, he is on the roster. World Series hero Will Klein (right elbow discomfort) has faced hitters, but he has not pitched in a game since July 31 and is viewed as more of a depth option. Blake Treinen (right shoulder inflammation) is unlikely to pitch this postseason.
Brewers: None.
Who is hot and who is not?
Dodgers: Freeman (.267, two homers), Muncy (.250, three homers) and Tucker (.333) have been among L.A.'s most consistent hitters this postseason. Smith (.063) and Ohtani (.154) are looking to shake off slow starts at the plate.
Brewers: Contreras led the Majors with 24 RBIs in September, had a .933 OPS from Sept. 9 through the end of the regular season, and then stayed hot in the NLDS, slashing .375/.444/.750 with a pair of home runs against the Padres. The Brewers would love to get Turang going again. His .361 average and .475 on-base percentage led the Majors in September and his 1.077 OPS was in the top 10, but he went 2-for-16 in the NLDS.
Anything else fans might want to know?
- Besides the three previous NLCS matchups, the Brewers and Dodgers also met in the 2020 NL Wild Card Series. The Dodgers swept in two games.
- This is the seventh time that the NLCS has pitted the same teams in back-to-back seasons. That also happened in 2020-21 (Braves and Dodgers), 2016-17 (Cubs and Dodgers), 2008-09 (Dodgers and Phillies), 2004-05 (Astros and Cardinals), 1991-92 (Braves and Pirates) and 1977-78 (Dodgers and Phillies).
- The Brewers are one of five teams -- along with the Mariners, Padres, Rays and Rockies -- that has never won the World Series.

Dodgers make Tarik Skubal decision that should worry Brewers before NLCS showdown originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Los Angeles Dodgers are four victories away from returning to the World Series, and manager Dave Roberts has revealed how his team plans to attack the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series.
Roberts announced Friday that Tarik Skubal will start Game 1 on Sunday, with Yoshinobu Yamamoto scheduled to pitch Game 2 on Monday. The decision gives Los Angeles two of baseball's most accomplished pitchers to begin a series that features the National League's top two regular-season teams.
The announcement also provides another reminder of the extraordinary pitching depth the Dodgers have assembled. Los Angeles is attempting to win its third consecutive World Series championship, and its starting rotation could become the biggest obstacle standing between Milwaukee and its own championship ambitions.
Tarik Skubal gets another opportunity to set the tone
Skubal will take the mound Sunday at American Family Field after delivering an excellent performance against the Atlanta Braves in the Division Series. The two-time Cy Young Award winner allowed one run on two hits over six innings in Game 1, striking out seven batters while issuing two walks.
Tarik Skubal will start Game 1 with Yoshinobu Yamamoto starting Game 2 for the Dodgers in the NLCS against the Brewers, per @ByJackHarris https://t.co/e8wI91D6uF
— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) October 9, 2026
Los Angeles acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers in a blockbuster August trade, adding another established ace to an already talented pitching staff. His arrival strengthened a rotation that included Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, giving Roberts multiple options capable of controlling a postseason game.
Starting Skubal in Game 1 is an important decision because Milwaukee owns home-field advantage in the series. The Brewers finished the regular season with 103 victories, while the Dodgers reached the 100-win mark. A strong opening performance would allow Los Angeles to immediately put pressure on a team that has been extremely difficult to beat throughout the year.
Skubal's ability to limit baserunners and generate strikeouts could be particularly valuable against a Milwaukee lineup featuring Christian Yelich, Jackson Chourio and William Contreras.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto gives Dodgers another major advantage
Yamamoto will follow Skubal in Game 2 after producing one of the Dodgers' best pitching performances against Atlanta. The right-hander struck out 10 batters over seven innings, allowing only one run on four hits in a victory that helped Los Angeles regain control of the Division Series.
The performance continued an impressive postseason history for Yamamoto, who earned World Series MVP honors in 2025. His ability to deliver deep, efficient outings gives Roberts another dependable option before the series shifts to Dodger Stadium. Milwaukee is expected to rely heavily on its own talented young pitchers, including Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson. The Brewers have demonstrated throughout the season that they can compete with baseball's most talented rosters, but matching Los Angeles on the mound will be a significant challenge.
The Dodgers also have decisions remaining beyond their first two starters. Roberts indicated Friday that the team was considering adding another pitcher to its NLCS roster, a move that would require removing a position player.
Dodgers still have questions despite pitching advantage
One concern involves veteran utility player Miguel Rojas, who left Game 3 against Atlanta because of lower back discomfort. Rojas participated in baseball activities Friday, but Roberts stopped short of confirming his availability for the championship series.
The Dodgers eliminated Atlanta in four games, while Milwaukee also advanced with a four-game victory over San Diego. The teams now meet in the NLCS for the second consecutive postseason, creating another opportunity for the Brewers to challenge the defending champions. Game 1 is scheduled for Sunday at 8 p.m. ET, with Game 2 following Monday at 5 p.m. ET.
Los Angeles has plenty of offensive talent, including Shohei Ohtani, but its starting pitching could determine how this series unfolds. By sending Skubal and Yamamoto to the mound in Milwaukee, Roberts is giving the Dodgers an opportunity to establish control before returning home.

SAN DIEGO -- It sure felt like forever since Christian Yelich notched a postseason RBI. And it was way too long before Brice Turang got his first hit against the Padres in this National League Division Series.
Still, the Brewers will need to get more from both players to help them advance to the next round, and perhaps beyond, after being handed a 4-3 loss in Tuesday's Game 3 as the Padres stayed alive for another day and now trail, 2-1, in the best-of-five series.
One of several missed opportunities for Milwaukee came in the fifth inning. The Brewers had already scored a tying run and then had the bases loaded and two outs when Turang grounded softly to shortstop Xander Bogaerts for a fielder's choice to keep from adding on.
"Trying to get a good pitch to hit. Just didn’t work out," Turang said. "It’s all right. We’ve got to move on and go win tomorrow."
That out made Turang 0-for-10 in the series and 2-for-40 (.050) with 14 strikeouts over his last 11 postseason games. The hitless skid ended when he lofted a two-out single to left field just out of reach for a diving Jase Bowen in the seventh inning.
"I’ve hit some balls right to people and had some good at-bats. I’ve just got to keep working, keep pushing forward," Turang said. "You just want to get better every day."
Yelich, the recently minted team captain and Milwaukee's longest-tenured star, picked up Turang by scorching a 107.2 mph liner to left-center field for an RBI single. It was his first RBI in a playoff game since his first-inning home run in Game 7 of the 2018 NL Championship Series vs. the Dodgers in a losing effort.
Both hitters got another chance to come through for Milwaukee in the top of the ninth inning. Turang worked a walk against Padres pitcher Michael King to put runners on first and second base with one out.
Yelich followed by blistering a first-pitch slider from King at 107.1 mph, only to see it one-hop directly to Bogaerts at shortstop, who turned the game-ending double play.
"A step to the right or left, it's pretty good," Yelich said. "I hit it hard. Just happened to be right at them. It's unfortunate. Part of the game. It's just how it goes sometimes. You've just got to keep battling. Not much else you can do. It is frustrating when it doesn't really bounce your way, but that's how it goes."
Although he’s driven in just the one run in this series, Yelich is batting .400 (4-for-10) with a double. He got the Brewers' first hit in all three games, and in the Game 2 thriller he drew a one-out walk that led to Jackson Chourio's two-run, walk-off single.
"He's looked great," Brewers hitting coach Eric Theisen said. "He's been on time. He's had some hard contact. As a team, we've had hard contact and some loud outs."
As for Turang, he was the Major League leader for September in average (.361) and on-base percentage (.475) before hitting the schneid in October.
"I think he's working his process, same as he always does, working his ABs," Theisen said. "We've seen some good swings. We've seen him put together some good ABs. The results haven't come. But he's continuing to work day to day the same way he always does. I still think he's in a good spot. Keep plugging away."
Sometimes a hit -- even a soft one -- can break the spell, but Theisen didn't put too much stock in Turang's bloop single.
"It's great that the ball falls and you get a knock and get on base. But the pitch-to-pitch approach and the way he's navigating at-bats is what's important," Theisen said. "The process is what's important."
Milwaukee left 11 men on base and missed multiple opportunities to take control of the game that would have given them an NLDS sweep. Besides Turang and Yelich, Chourio went 0-for-4 with a fifth-inning sacrifice fly. He was robbed of a hit by center fielder Jackson Merrill's great catch on the warning track to open the game. Bauers went 0-for-4 with four strikeouts and a walk.
"We had some really good at-bats, hit the ball hard, put ourselves in a good position to win the game. Sometimes you just need that big hit. We’ve got to focus on winning tomorrow," Turang said. "The quality of at-bats that we’ve had has been really cool to see. We’ll get it going. I trust everybody in this locker room."
Said Theisen: "Not everybody's been hot all year long, and it seems like the lineup is deep. When one or two guys have a stretch of games or two or three where maybe they're not producing like they always do, somebody steps up and does it. That's the beautiful thing about this offense and what we've shown all year."
Now the Brewers need to show it in Game 4.

item.content:encoded:
The Athletic has live coverage of the MLB Playoffs, including the ALDS Game 2s of White Sox vs Guardians and Yankees vs Rays.
After three days of Wild Card Series action, the dust has settled and four teams (Houston Astros, Boston Red Sox, Philadelphia Phillies and Chicago Cubs) have found themselves on an early vacation. Major League Baseball’s 12-team postseason field has been whittled to eight.
Now, the race for the World Series shifts to the next round: the Division Series. Four teams (Cleveland Guardians, Los Angeles Dodgers, Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers) that had first-round byes will now be in action. Additionally, while the Wild Card Series featured a best-of-three format, the Division Series will be best-of-five.
Here’s how MLB’s bracket looks right now:
You can watch the MLB playoffs on Fubo (Stream Free Now).
What is Saturday’s MLB Playoff schedule and starters?
White Sox at Guardians (AL Division Series Game 1): Hagen Smith vs. Parker Messick
First pitch: 1 p.m. ET (TBS)
After the 23-year-old Smith pitched three scoreless innings in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series against the Astros, the White Sox turn to him for an encore performance in Game 1 of the ALDS. While the club was able to pile on six runs against the Astros in a win, it won’t be as easy against the Guardians and Messick.
An All-Star this season, Messick finished his rookie campaign with a 2.56 ERA and 193 strikeouts over 32 starts. Against the White Sox, Messick carded a 2.81 ERA in four starts (25 2/3 innings).
Braves at Dodgers (NL Division Series Game 1): TBD vs. Tarik Skubal
First pitch: 4 p.m. ET (Fox)
Having burned Chris Sale to take Thursday’s winner-take-all game against the Phillies, and with Tyler Mahle also unavailable, the Braves appear to be looking at another bullpen game.
“They’ve pitched in big situations during the season, and no matter who we really see right now in that bullpen in any situation, no matter what inning it is, we’re feeling pretty confident about them,” catcher Drake Baldwin told reporters.
The Dodgers, coming off a first-round bye, will counter with Tarik Skubal, the crown jewel acquisition of this year’s trade deadline. The AL’s reigning Cy Young Award winner has a 2.61 ERA with his new team, his final starts before reaching a highly anticipated free agency.
Yankees at Rays (AL Division Series Game 1): Gerrit Cole vs. Drew Rasmussen
First pitch: 6:30 p.m. ET (TBS)
Faced with an embarrassment of riches on the pitching side, the Yankees will deploy 2023 AL Cy Young Award winner Gerrit Cole against the AL East champs. After Cole in Game 1, the Yankees will have Cam Schlittler in Game 2 and some variation of Max Fried or Carlos Rodón in Games 3 and 4, the last matchup only if necessary.
On the Tampa Bay side, Drew Rasmussen, arguably one of the most underrated aces in the sport, will get the ball at Tropicana Field. For his career, Rasmussen has a 1.81 ERA in 11 games (10 starts) against the Yankees.
Padres at Brewers (NL Division Series Game 1): Robbie Ray vs. Jacob Misiorowski
First pitch: 8:30 p.m. ET (FS1)
Saturday’s final matchup will feature two pitchers at opposite ends of their careers. On the San Diego side, Robbie Ray, the 2021 AL Cy Young Award winner, has been largely unable to replicate the success he had that season. After a deadline trade from the San Francisco Giants to the Padres, Ray has carded a 5.02 ERA over nine starts.
For the Brewers, Jacob Misiorowski is just getting started. An All-Star in his rookie year, Misiorowski finished his sophomore campaign as the favorite to win the NL Cy Young Award, leading MLB with a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts. He’s wowed the sport with his ability to repeatedly fire fastballs in excess of 100 mph, and there’s reason to believe that, at 24 years old, his best is yet to come.
What to know about each Division Series matchup
White Sox at Guardians: The two AL Central clubs played each other 13 times during the regular season, with the White Sox winning the season series 7-6. That, however, was not enough to overcome a late surge by the Guardians and a collapse by Chicago that led to the White Sox losing control of the division and having to play their way out of the wild card.
Now, the two clubs will meet again for at least three games, a spot in the Championship Series on the line. By winning the division and finishing with a better record than the AL West winner, the Guardians were granted a first-round bye. No mind, the White Sox dispatched the Astros in two games and have been off since Thursday. That extra rest has allowed the club to realign its depleted pitching staff.
One thing to watch: How Chicago’s thin, matchup-dependent pitching staff is deployed against Cleveland’s newfound offense — the club led the AL in wRC+ (108) from Aug. 1 onward. The urgency, or lack thereof, by White Sox manager Will Venable could swing the series either direction.
Braves at Dodgers: The Braves’ pitching staff will enter Game 1 with very little margin for error, as it will likely be a group effort without a starter available. That alone could be the difference, as teams that take Game 1 in any best-of-five series have historically won the series 72 percent of the time. That said, these Dodgers have not played their best against the Braves, losing the season series 5-1, including a late-August sweep when Tyler Glasnow and Yoshinobu Yamamoto both pitched.
One thing to watch: Shohei Ohtani’s ability to contribute. The four-time MVP has spent much of the second half of the season compromised, leading to an abbreviated September, with some of it on the injured list.
“I do feel like my swing is in a better place, feels smooth, and just a little tweaks here and there, and I’ll be ready for tomorrow,” Ohtani said through interpreter Will Ireton.
Yankees at Rays: Only one team had a better record over its final 30 games than the Rays, who went 20-10 to fend off a late Yankees push to claim the AL East. That, plus a 55-26 home record that tied the Brewers for the best in MLB, has Tampa Bay inching toward its first World Series appearance since 2020. To get there, the Rays will need to beat the Yankees, who made quick work of the Red Sox in the wild-card round. That they did so without Aaron Judge on the roster or needing to call on Giancarlo Stanton in a pinch hit capacity is all the more impressive.
One thing to watch: Junior Caminero was 20 years old the last time the Rays made the postseason, going hitless in two at-bats. Since then, Caminero, now 23, has morphed into a perennial All-Star, hitting 40 home runs in consecutive seasons, the latter of which should earn him major MVP consideration. Few players love the big stage as much as Caminero. One of those players just so happens to be Cam Schlittler, the presumptive AL Cy Young Award winner, who will take the ball at least once this series. How these two match up will be one of the best subplots of this postseason.
Padres at Brewers: In a battle between arguably MLB’s hottest team (the Padres) and the league’s best team all season (the Brewers), there will be a lot of firsts. This is San Diego’s first Division Series under new owners José E. Feliciano and his wife and business partner Kwanza Jones. It will be the first extended runway for Padres rookie catcher Ethan Salas. It will be the first postseason series for Christian Yelich as the Brewers’ captain. And it will be the first time Misiorowski faces these Padres since May.
Should Milwaukee win, it will be the first time in franchise history that the club has made it to back-to-back league championship series. If San Diego upsets MLB’s No. 1 team, it will be the club’s first trip since 2022 and just its fourth overall.
One thing to watch: The bullpens. Behind multiple high-leverage arms, San Diego has made the late innings nearly impossible for opposing teams. If there’s one club that can match the Padres in that regard, it’s the Brewers. The late innings will likely be the deciding factor in who advances.
