The Milwaukee Brewers have an unfortunate history of late-season injuries preceding postseason runs. September injuries to Christian Yelich and Brandon Woodruff are the most recent examples, but the trend also extends to Devin Williams breaking his hand after punching a wall in 2021, Ben Sheets not being a part of the 2008 postseason run after a flexor tendon injury, and of course, Rollie Fingers' forearm injury ahead of the team's memorable 1982 run.
With just over 24 hours remaining until the Brewers' 2026 postseason opener, this year's team thankfully hasn't made a contribution to that disheartening list. However, as the Brewers finish out their stretch of five days off -- the result of them earning a first-round bye -- there was an injury scare that had Brewers fans feeling déjà vu.
Infielder Joey Ortiz exited the Brewers' Friday night opener in their final series of the regular season with a noticeable limp. After the game, manager Pat Murphy revealed that Ortiz had been battling soreness in his knee due to a bruise he sustained during the team's series against the Philadelphia Phillies and also some inflammation in his abdomen that has been causing him discomfort.
Ortiz didn't play either of the final two games of the regular season, and his postseason roster status was briefly in doubt when Murphy couldn't commit one way or another on Tuesday afternoon. However, thankfully, during Friday's media availability, the Brewers' manager took a more optimistic tone when talking about his injured infielder. Said Murphy on Ortiz on Friday afternoon, "It looks like it's progressing in the right direction...I would say at this point we're planning on him being available."
The Brewers are planning on Joey Ortiz "being available" for the NLDS
Despite his struggles during the 2025 season and first half of the 2026 campaign, Ortiz became one of the Brewers' most productive hitters during the second half of this year. In fact, Ortiz had the ninth best OPS (.883) among NL hitters with at least 200 plate appearances, from July 1 to the end of the season. As crazy as the statement would have sounded during the middle of May, Ortiz is one of the Brewers' key offensive X-factors heading into the postseason.
Therefore, it would have been a significant blow had Ortiz missed out on the 2026 postseason run due to his late-season knee and abdomen injuries, but thankfully the Brewers' infielder is expected to be available tomorrow night.
Ortiz's production would indicate that he should start every game regardless of the handedness of the opposing pitcher, but Murphy consistently used David Hamilton against tough right-handed starters at third base, so it's not yet certain just how many games Joey O will start in the postseason. That said, the Padres just announced that southpaw Robbie Ray is getting the ball in Game 1, so Ortiz will almost certainly be manning the hot corner on Saturday night. Regardless of how many at-bats Murphy gives his surging third baseman in October, it's undeniably a welcome development that Ortiz will likely be available for the NLDS roster.

item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong was in a sort of mini-funk. The All-Star center fielder had gone 3 for his previous 20 with seven strikeouts and no extra-base hits and the Cubs were headed into a mid-September three-game series against the eventual NL East champion Braves. He was still the overwhelming favorite to win the National League MVP, but things hadn't been going right.
He popped out in foul territory in his first at-bat. Next time up, PCA sent a rocket double down the right-field line. And it was, as they say, on. He finished the game with four hits, including a home run, and four RBI. Two nights later, he went 3 for 4 with a triple and two home runs. In a single series against a playoff team, he had one four-hit game and another 11-base game.
"When he hit the second homer, Alex Bregman was standing next to me," Cubs manager Craig Counsell said after the two-home run game (via MLB.com). "I said, 'Alex, we don't get to see things like this.' You spend your whole life in baseball and you just don't see this happen on a baseball field. You're grateful to be a part of it.
"You're grateful to see things like this. And you're grateful that the fans get to see a season like this, because they're going to talk about it. They're going to tell their kids about it. They're going to tell their grandkids about seasons like this."
Bregman has seen plenty of elite-level play, too. The two-time World Series champion and four-time pennant winner played with 2017 American League MVP José Altuve and finished second himself in 2019. He was in the same division as Mike Trout for nine years. And Counsell is telling him about how special this is?
Counsell would know, too. As a player, he won the World Series with the 1997 Marlins and 2001 Diamondbacks. He was teammates with Ryan Braun during his 2011 MVP campaign and came up with the Rockies in the '90s while Larry Walker was in his prime. He also managed Christian Yelich during his MVP season in 2018.
And still, he sees something special in Crow-Armstrong.
The younger guys are taking notice, too.
"As far as the seasons I've seen in my experience in professional baseball, this is the best," Cubs utility infielder Matt Shaw told CBS Sports. "I don't think I've seen anything that even compares."
Crow-Armstrong finished his magical 2026 season on Sunday when he was removed for a pinch runner after singling to start the game. The final line: .280/.372/.570 (155 OPS+) with 31 doubles, eight triples, 45 home runs, 107 RBI, 119 runs, 41 steals, 9.8 bWAR, 10.6 fWAR and some of the best defensive stats in baseball. He was the seventh player in MLB history to reach the .
It was one of the very best individual seasons in Cubs history.
The origin story
Through June 24, 2021, the Cubs were sitting in a first-place tie thanks to a roster largely made up of their 2016 World Series heroes. After throwing a combined no-hitter in Dodger Stadium, the Cubs proceeded to lose three straight games. They headed to Milwaukee on June 28 to start a three-game series. They were outscored 41-8 in a Brewers sweep, with Counsell at the helm as Milwaukee's skipper.
This was the start of the end for that 2021 Cubs team, which completely fell apart and eventually saw the front office tear up the 2016 nucleus and move on. Kris Bryant and Anthony Rizzo were traded, as was fan favorite Javier Báez to the Mets in a deal that also included pitcher Trevor Williams. In return came a 19-year-old kid named Pete Crow-Armstrong.
Crow-Armstrong wasn't some obscure tack-on on whom the Cubs got lucky. He had been drafted No. 19 out of high school the year prior. His upside was well known.
Still, he had only six games of professional experience before falling injured that season. There was upside to dream on, but also a lot of unknown.
PCA debuted late in 2023 and looked overmatched at the plate, going 0 for 14 with seven strikeouts. Still, heading into 2024, he was a consensus top-20 prospect in all of baseball. The projections were that he'd be elite in center field, elite on the bases and had a decent chance to become a good hitter. Maybe something like a .275 average, .340 on-base percentage and 15-20 homers would become a normal season.
He showed flashes on offense in 2024, especially given that he was only 22 years old, but failed to live up to expectations.
Then there was the first-half breakout in 2025, followed by a disaster of a second half at the plate. The eye test said he was a totally different hitter. The splits line up:
1st half: .265/.302/.544
2nd half: .216/.262/.372
The poor plate performance carried over into 2026. He was only hitting .224/.314/.362 through May 29. And then, amid "overrated" chants from Cardinals fans in St. Louis, he went deep and took off for the rest of the season.
From that game through the end of the season, Crow-Armstrong hit .308 with an OBP above .400, slugged nearly .700 and clubbed 39 home runs in 104 games. One of the biggest differences has been his grasp of the strike zone, cutting down on swinging at bad pitches and doing damage on strikes.
Sure enough, his walk rate rose from 4.5% last season to 11.4% this year. He reduced the rate at which he swung at pitches outside the strike zone by more than 7 points. He swung roughly 10% less overall. His hard-hit percentage went from 41.6 to 48.5. Again, the formula: Swing less, swing at fewer bad pitches, do more damage when you do swing.
It sounds simple, but it's a difficult adjustment at the big-league level, and many young players never pull it off. PCA did it at age 24 and turned into one of the best players in baseball.
"Absolutely," Crow-Armstrong told CBS Sports when asked if he thought this type of season was possible. "That's what I work for."
A jaw-dropping 2026 season
Crow-Armstrong's 40-40 season made him just the seventh player ever to pull off the feat. He had seven four-hit games this season, leading the majors (Jackson Chourio was second with six).
He led the majors in runs scored. He was sixth in hits and tied for fifth in triples. He tied former Cubs (and current Phillies) slugger Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead in home runs. He tied for fourth in steals. He led a handful of defensive metrics.
And, despite being a primary leadoff man, PCA finished fourth in the majors in RBI.
The list of primary leadoff men who topped 100 RBI in a season is awfully short. PCA didn't hit leadoff all season, but he racked up 83 RBI in only 107 games from that position. Shohei Ohtani's 84 in 90 games is one of the few seasons with more bulk at a higher rate per game. The record is 107 from Mookie Betts in 2023, and that was in 151 games from the leadoff spot. Still, to finish fourth in RBI despite leading off over 100 times is ridiculous.
Remember that 11-base game? He reached 10 total bases six times this season, tying the MLB record along with 2019 Nelson Cruz (only 1997 Larry Walker, 1940 Johnny Mize and 1933 Jimmie Foxx even had five such games in a season).
How about if we cherry-pick the numbers and go with 45 home runs, eight triples and 30 doubles in a season? Crow-Armstrong did that this year. The others who have done so? Babe Ruth (twice), Lou Gehrig (twice), Jimmie Foxx (three times), Joe DiMaggio and Eddie Mathews. That's it. Mathews and PCA are the only two to get there since integration, and PCA is the only player since 1953.
And even as the bat has leveled up, the defense and baserunning haven't lagged behind at all. He's become an all-around force, and that shows up in WAR. Crow-Armstrong led the majors in both major versions of WAR. In FanGraphs' metric, it wasn't even remotely close: Bobby Witt Jr. finished second among position players at 6.9. PCA had 10.6.
In fact, if we stick with FanGraphs' WAR, the only seasons higher this century than PCA's 2026 are three Barry Bonds seasons and two Aaron Judge seasons. That's it. He's topped the best career mark posted by Albert Pujols, Alex Rodriguez, Mike Trout, Miguel Cabrera, Mookie Betts, Ronald Acuña Jr., Shohei Ohtani and, well, everyone else but Bonds and Judge.
The Cubs have been around since 1876. The only player to post a higher fWAR in a season in franchise history than PCA did this season was Rogers Hornsby in 1929. Yes, this Pete Crow-Armstrong season rated higher via this metric than anything from Ernie Banks, Ron Santo, Billy Williams, Ryne Sandberg and Sammy Sosa.
Again, the defensive and baserunning chops were always going to be there. It's the offensive strides that made him special this season.
What's next?
"That'll be a never-ending process," Crow-Armstrong told CBS Sports earlier this month when asked what improvements his game needs. "I view it as, if I can do this now, I still carry the belief that I have more in me and, yeah, there's always going to be things I can get better at and I would hope that's how my career goes. That would be a very lucky way to be able to experience this game -- just experiencing yourself growing every year. That's really what I've come to notice the most this year is that I've been very aware of growth."
For Crow-Armstrong, everything is about the greater goal: winning, and winning as a team.
"We're here to win baseball games, we're not here to show up and reach individual milestones," he said. "Those just happen by playing good baseball."
He's done plenty of that in 2026. Now the focus will be on helping the Cubs to their first deep playoff run since 2017.

item.content:encoded:
Back in July, we celebrated the All-Star Game by looking at which participants had the best chance of eventually earning induction into the Hall of Fame. The likes of Bryce Harper, Justin Verlander, and Mike Trout all were locks, and rightfully so.
But as the MLB playoffs prepare to kick off, Verlander and Trout are once again sitting at home. Harper and the Phillies survived a near-collapse to secure a Wild Card seed, and he’s one of many postseason participants who could — and in his case, should — find themselves in the Hall of Fame one day.
Besides the obvious counting stats, what makes a Hall of Famer? As we’ve previously noted, baseball fans have recently accepted 40 bWAR as the standard for a remarkable career. Immaculate Grid is to thank on that front, even if there are players who have cleared that mark but don’t feel like Hall of Famers. Astros shortstop Carlos Correa, who is injured but has a 47.1 bWAR, is a perfect example, and he didn’t crack our list.
Instead, let’s turn our attention to someone who may very well become the second unanimous electee when his time comes.
Honorable mention: The Shohei Ohtani tier
Barring any unprecedented rule changes, Hall of Fame candidates must have 10 full seasons worth of experience for eligibility. That means Shohei Ohtani would technically be ineligible if he retired tomorrow, so he won’t land in the “lock” tier.
But Ohtani has always been a unicorn, so him having his own category makes all too much sense. We can all agree that, at this time next year, Ohtani should be a lock on that list.
Not yet eligible, but…
These guys don’t get their own table, but we wanted to address their situations ahead of the playoffs.
- Aroldis Chapman, P, Boston Red Sox: Off the numbers alone, Chapman and his 402 saves (ninth all-time) likely warrant induction. However, he also served a 30-game suspension in 2016 for violating the league’s domestic violence policy. It’s difficult to envision him earning the 75 percent required for election. Recent voting trends don’t work in favor of those who have been suspended for performance-enhancing drugs (more on that soon) or off-field incidents.
- Cam Schlittler, SP, New York Yankees and Jacob Misirowski, SP, Milwaukee Brewers: We’re lumping these two together because both will be trending during the playoffs. Just because these two are likely to win their league’s respective Cy Young Awards doesn’t mean they’re guaranteed a spot in Cooperstown. Heck, we don’t even know if they’ll pitch long enough to appear on a ballot! But, you know how baseball fans are.
- Fernando Tatis Jr., 2B/RF, San Diego Padres: As things currently stand, Tatis has no chance of getting into the Hall of Fame. Voters have made it clear that those who serve PED-related suspensions, as Tatis did in 2022, aren’t welcome in Cooperstown unless they buy a ticket. That said, we’re including him here
- Tarik Skubal, SP, Los Angeles Dodgers: Skubal became the 23rd pitcher in MLB history to win multiple Cy Young Awards, which will appeal to voters who prefer the "dominant" peak. But we’d like to see at least two or three more years of him being at least above-average. He’s also only seven seasons in, so he has a lot of work left.
On pace to make it into Cooperstown
- Alex Bregman, Chicago Cubs - 48.9 bWAR
- Matt Olson, Atlanta Braves - 44.2 bWAR
- Yordan Alvarez, DH, Houston Astros - 30.5 bWAR
These three have team success, specifically at least one World Series ring, working in their favor. Alvarez is likely to win AL MVP, and the 29-year-old is young enough that clearing 40 bWAR shouldn’t be an issue so long as healthy.
Bregman turns 33 next March, and his bWAR is likely far greater than you’d have guessed. But is he truly on a Hall of Fame trajectory? He's nowhere close to 2,000 hits (1,411) or 300 home runs (237), both of which are vital numbers when playing the hot corner.
Consider, though, that Bregman has averaged 24 home runs, 84 RBIs, 32 doubles, and 4.6 bWAR over the last five years. He’s under contract through 2030, and exceeded all of those numbers (28 home runs, 93 RBIs, 33 doubles, and 5.8 bWAR) this season.
If Bregman were to continue averaging those numbers, he’d end the 2031 season with 333 home runs, roughly 2,200 hits, and 481 doubles. Oh, and his bWAR would be right around 72.0, so we imagine he’d be a first-ballot inductee.
Unfortunately for him and Olson, the possibility of a work stoppage could have a monumental impact on their final counting stats. Which leads us into…
Borderline veterans
- Giancarlo Stanton, New York Yankees - 47.0 bWAR
- Zack Wheeler, Philadelphia Phillies - 46.6 bWAR
- Gerrit Cole, SP, New York Yankees - 45.8 bWAR
- Christian Yelich, Milwaukee Brewers - 45.1 bWAR
- Xander Bogaerts, SS, San Diego Padres - 44.3 bWAR
- Max Fried, P, New York Yankees - 32.3 bWAR
- Kyle Schwarber, OF/DH, Philadelphia Phillies - 22.3 bWAR
Stanton and Schwarber’s cases are likely dependent on whether they surpass 500 home runs. The latter will enter next season at 385 homers, and he turns 34 in March. But the looming work stoppage could significantly affect his chances of reaching 400 anytime soon.
As for Stanton, multiple lower-body injuries limited him to three homers in 24 games. Although he has 466 career home runs, the 2017 NL MVP turns 37 in November and is a free agent after next year.
The only members of the 500-home run club who aren’t in the Hall of Fame are either ineligible or have ties to performance-enhancing drugs. It’d be pretty remarkable if Schwarber and Stanton both cleared the historic total yet fell short of Cooperstown.
Personally, Wheeler and Cole are probably the only ones who will have a legitimate Hall of Fame résumé when they become eligible. The rest of those guys are Hall of Very Good at best. Much like Skubal, we need two or three more elite seasons from Fried before we’d even consider voting for him.
Go ahead and make the Hall of Fame plaque
- Mookie Betts, Los Angeles Dodgers - 79.0 bWAR
- Freddie Freeman, Los Angeles Dodgers - 66.8 bWAR
- Paul Goldschmidt, New York Yankees - 65.1 bWAR
- Aaron Judge, New York Yankees - 64.2 bWAR
- Manny Machado, San Diego Padres - 63.3 bWAR
- Chris Sale, Atlanta Braves - 62.7 bWAR
- José Ramírez, Cleveland Guardians - 60.3 bWAR
- Bryce Harper, Philadelphia Phillies - 56.9 bWAR
- Jose Altuve, Houston Astros - 53.4 bWAR
Outside of Goldschmidt and Sale, none of these names are overly surprising. And no, the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal shouldn’t impact Altuve, especially not after Carlos Beltrán just entered the Hall of Fame.
Goldschmidt currently ranks 143rd on the all-time bWAR list, and only 31 men above him aren’t already enshrined. But of the 20 who are or were eligible, most came up short for PED or off-field reasons. The question then becomes whether he’s wearing a Diamondbacks or Cardinals cap, or if he opts for the blank hat.
Although Sale turns 38 next March, he has a lifetime 2.95 ERA and 2,779 strikeouts, putting him within range of reaching 3,000. There’s absolutely no reason why he shouldn’t be a first-ballot selection.
As for the rest? You know a Hall of Famer when you see one, and they more than meet the expectations.

MILWAUKEE — Team captains are not common in Major League Baseball. But on Saturday, the Milwaukee Brewers named Christian Yelich the first captain in franchise history, making him one of only three active captains in the majors.
The Brewers decided in a team meeting prior to its Saturday game against the St. Louis Cardinals to give the honor to Yelich. But Yelich did not want to accept without “sign-off” from another Brewers legend: Robin Yount.
Yelich requested that Yount, who played his entire 20-year career with Milwaukee, sign off on his captaincy before accepting. Yount, a Hall of Famer, was a leader on the only Brewers’ team to make the World Series in 1982.
Yount joined Wisconsin’s Midday News to discuss the conversations he had with Yelich and Brewers Manager Pat Murphy ahead of Saturday’s announcement.
“In all honesty, they certainly didn’t need my approval,” Yount said. “But in saying that, it was very, very humbling to be honest, to think that they would even consider asking me what I thought.”
Yount said the fact that he was asked speaks to the character of this team, calling them a “class act, especially at this time of the season.”
While Yount has not been around the current Brewers team as much as in previous years, he said he got to know Yelich through their mutual friend, Bob Uecker.
“I learned a lot about Christian through the years Ueck was around him,” Yount said. “Ueck spoke of Christian in the highest regard… The team pretty much looked up to him as that guy. And that’s all I needed to hear from somebody that was around him enough.”

Jacob Misiorowski strengthened his Cy Young case, allowing just two hits over five-plus scoreless innings, as the Milwaukee Brewers built momentum for the postseason with a 6-4 victory over the visiting St. Louis Cardinals on Sunday.
Milwaukee (103-59), which has clinched a first-round Wild Card bye and home-field advantage throughout the playoffs, closed with five consecutive wins to extend its franchise record for victories in a season.
Milwaukee, the first team to win four consecutive NL Central titles, finished 35-17 against division rivals and went 18-6 in September.
St. Louis (77-85) scored four runs in the eighth off Chad Patrick to pull within 6-4, capped by Leo Bernal’s three-run homer. Shane Drohan got the final five outs for his second save.
Misiorowski (16-5) allowed two singles in 5 1/3 innings, departing after striking out Jordan Walker in the sixth to end a 68-pitch outing, lowering his major league-leading ERA to 1.80. Misiorowski struck out five and walked two, giving him 252 strikeouts for the year.
Misiorowski is the second Brewers pitcher to lead the league in ERA, joining Corbin Burnes (2021).
Milwaukee bunched six singles off Andre Pallante in the first inning for a 3-0 lead. Garrett Mitchell, Jake Bauers and Jackson Chourio opened with consecutive singles for the first run. Brice Turang reached on a run-scoring infield single, giving him 100 RBIs for the season. Christian Yelich singled in another run.
Gary Sanchez put the Brewers up 5-0 with one out in the third with his 12th home run following a leadoff single by Chourio.
Chourio’s RBI single in the fourth made it 6-0.
St. Louis rallied in the eighth when Cesar Prieto triple to open and Pedro Pages walked. Prieto scored on Jordan Walker’s fielder’s choice grounder. Ivan Herrera walked and Bernal followed with his fifth homer.
Pallante (12-9) allowed six runs on 10 hits in five innings, striking out four and walking one.
St. Louis, which has not made the postseason since 2022 and has not won a playoff series since the NLDS in 2019, was 50-45 at the All-Star break, but went 27-40 the rest of the way.
–Field Level Media

MILWAUKEE (AP) — Jacob Misiorowski allowed two hits in 5 1/3 shutout innings to cap his brilliant season as the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the St. Louis Cardinals 6-4 on Sunday.
The Brewers improved to 103-59 and closed the regular season with five straight victories, matching their longest streak of the season. The Brewers’ 103 wins broke the franchise record they had set a year earlier when they went 97-65.
Milwaukee has home-field advantage throughout the postseason as it gears up for its eighth playoff appearance in nine years.
St. Louis closed a fourth straight non-playoff season with a 77-85 record, one game worse than the Cardinals’ finish last year.
Misiorowski (16-5) struck out five and walked two while improving his ERA to 1.80, the best in the majors. Misiorowski also has an MLB-leading 252 strikeouts.
Milwaukee gave Misiorowski an early 3-0 lead when Cardinals starter Andre Pallante allowed singles to six of the first seven batters he faced. Jackson Chourio, Brice Turang and Christian Yelich each hit an RBI single.
Turang’s infield hit brought home Jake Bauers for his 100th RBI of the season. Six of them came during this weekend sweep.
Turang became the eighth player in Brewers history to have at least 100 runs and 100 RBIs in a season. Ryan Braun accomplished the feat four times. Robin Yount, Cecil Cooper and Prince Fielder did it twice each. The others are Jeromy Burnitz and John Jaha.
Gary Sánchez hit a two-run homer in the third and Chourio added a two-out RBI single in the fourth to extend the lead to 6-0. Chourio went 3 for 4.
St. Louis scored all four of its runs in the eighth inning off Chad Patrick. Leo Bernal highlighted that outburst with a three-run homer.
Shane Drohan retired the side in order in the ninth to earn his second save.
Pallante (12-9) allowed six runs and 10 hits in five innings.
Up next
The NL Central champion Brewers will host either the Chicago Cubs or San Diego Padres in the opening game of an NL Division Series on Saturday.

The Milwaukee Brewers are coming off a series victory over the Philadelphia Phillies that they wrapped up Thursday with a 5-1 victory.
Now, they’re back home Friday night. And continue to inch closer to clinching the No. 1 overall seed in the National League as they begin their final series of the regular season against the St. Louis Cardinals.
On Friday night, Milwaukee will have right-handed pitcher Robert Gasser on the mound against Cardinals righty Michael McGreevy.
Ahead of the matchup, Brewers manager Pat Murphy made a notable change to the starting lineup involving veteran slugger Christian Yelich.

Pete Crow-Armstrong is the favorite to win the National League MVP Award, and even his rivals have nothing but great things to say about him.
The Cubs once again fell short of winning the National League Central, watching the Brewers' four-peat for the first time in the division's history. The Brewers have their own MVP Award winner in Christian Yelich. Yelich won MVP in 2018 and was the favorite to win a second MVP Award in 2019 before a knee injury in the final month of the regular season.
It's been a while since Yelich won MVP, but at his peak he was a dynamic power-speed threat, just like Crow-Armstrong. Yelich didn't have the advantage that Crow-Armstrong does on the bases with all of the new rules, but he was still able to make a difference at the plate with his power and with his legs on the basepaths. Yelich acknowledged how good a hitter Crow-Armstrong has been this year, despite playing for his rival team.
"He's probably the best defender in the game right now, and it'd be hard to find another hitter that's going as good as he is," Yelich said, per ESPN's Jesse Rogers. "He's had a great year and a special year for him."
Yelich's MVP season was great, but it did not feature Platinum Glove defense.
"Yes, without the defense," Yelich said when asked if he sees similarities between his MVP season and Crow-Armstrong's. "That's what makes him really, really special -- is being able to combine the two."
Crow-Armstrong should win the Platinum Glove this year, and there's a good chance his Cubs and Yelich's Brewers meet in the postseason.

The Milwaukee Brewers have a 100-win season. With a victory over the Philadelphia Phillies on Thursday night, the 2026 Brew Crew improved to 100-59 on the 2026 season, reaching an unbelievable milestone that hadn't been accomplished in the first 57 seasons of the franchise's history.
After projection models expected the Brewers to finish with somewhere between 80-85 wins during the 2026 season, Pat Murphy's squad has proved the preseason predictions wrong once again. However, they didn't just surpass their expected win total by a few games; they blew past the projections, produced the best regular season in franchise history, and reached the elusive 100-win mark.
It's an unbelievable accomplishment, one that is made even more impressive by the fact that Milwaukee has produced 90+ win seasons in each of the last four seasons and five times in the last six years. This isn't a one-off season in which the Brewers sacrificed their future and went "all in" on one year. Rather, it's just another chapter in what has easily been the most successful stretch of seasons in franchise history. Put another way, to win 100 games with the best farm system in baseball makes the achievement that much more incredible.
It took a pair of wins over the Philadelphia Phillies, who still have plenty to play for, to achieve 100 wins before their final series of the regular season. With the Brewers fully in postseason preparation mode, made clear by a number of roster and in-game decisions, Murphy's team displayed their impressive depth in their late-September series victory over the Phillies. Said roster depth will be key in the postseason.
Brewers' rely on impressive roster depth to reach elusive 100-win mark after postseason preparation has begun
The Brewers entered Thursday night's series finale against the Phillies with a first-round bye, and therefore a spot in the NLDS, already secured. They didn't have nearly as much to play for as Philadelphia, who is fighting to secure home-field advantage in the Wild Card Series. As a result, Murphy turned to Shane Drohan, who is expected to be a reliever in October, for a short start, didn't include Christian Yelich or Jackson Chourio in the starting lineup, and opted to have William Contreras DH during the series finale on Thursday night. Murphy didn't use Abner Uribe or Trevor Megill and kept Antonio Senzatela in for a save in the ninth inning, and yet, even with their postseason preparation fully underway, the Brewers knocked off the mighty Phillies, who have not officially clinched a spot in the postseason just yet.
In other words, the Brewers won their 100th game of the season on Thursday night due to their impressive roster depth. Murphy's squad proved that they can defeat a postseason team like the Phillies without using one of their top starters, without starting Chourio or Yelich, and without turning to their elite high-leverage duo at the end of the ballgame.
That type of roster depth bodes well for Milwaukee's chances in October. A deep postseason run, like the one the Brewers are hoping to put together, requires contributions throughout the roster. Whether it be a pinch-hit appearance, escaping a jam in the middle innings, or serving as a defensive replacement late in the game, the 26 Brewers that Milwaukee elects to include on their postseason roster will each have their role. It's therefore encouraging to see so many of them contribute to the Brewers' late-season series win over the Phillies, which led to 100 wins.
The Brewers have three games left to improve their record-breaking regular season record even further. Expect a similar strategy, in which Murphy relies on his depth to give necessary rest to each of his players, in the Brewers' upcoming weekend series against the St. Louis Cardinals. That said, regardless of how the final series plays out, the 2026 Brewers officially have a 100-win season to their name -- a truly incredible accomplishment.

item.content:encoded:
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Christian Yelich and Brice Turang hit solo home runs, and the Milwaukee Brewers delayed Philadelphia’s potential postseason clinch with a 4-1 win over the Phillies on Wednesday night.
The Phillies needed both a win over the Brewers and a loss later Wednesday night by either Arizona or San Diego to secure their fifth straight trip to the National League playoffs. The Phillies started their run with a trip to the World Series in 2022, reached the NL Championship Series the next season and are coming off consecutive NL East titles.
The Phillies have to settle for a wild-card berth this season and are likely to open the playoffs next week on the road. The Phillies, Chicago and San Diego hold the three NL wild cards headed into the final games of the season.
The Phillies went 0 for 12 with runners in scoring position against the Brewers and left 10 runners on base.
Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said ahead of the game the team was willing to wait at Citizens Bank Park until after the Padres game ended, if necessary, to celebrate. No need to hang around.
Aaron Nola (7-11) had turned around a miserable season and posted a 1.86 ERA over his last eight starts as the longest-tenured Phillie got the chance to clinch. With a playoff party looming, he instead surrendered Turang’s 20th homer of the season in the first inning and Yelich’s 12th of the year in the second.
The Phillies scored their only run in the second inning after loading the bases with no outs against Brewers starter Logan Henderson (11-3). Henderson allowed four hits and one run over five innings to help the NL Central champion Brewers win their 99th game of the season.
Trevor Megill worked a scoreless ninth for his 30th save.
William Contreras extended his hitting streak to 11 games with a two-run single in the third for a 4-1 lead.
Nola struck out eight in six innings.
Up next
The Brewers did not announce a starter for Thursday's game. The Phillies send RHP Andrew Painter (3-10, 5.59 ERA) to the mound.

item.content:encoded:
Zack Wheeler walked out to the mound at Citizens Bank Park Tuesday night needing three strikeouts to reach 2,000. It took him 12 pitches. Garrett Mitchell went down first. Then Jackson Chourio and Brice Turang were rung up as Wheeler reached the milestone against the Milwaukee Brewers.
But, Wheeler kept going.
William Contreras, Jake Bauers and Christian Yelich struck out in the second. Luis Lara struck out to lead off the third inning. Wheeler struck out seven straight Brewers to start the game, something no Phillies pitcher had done to start a game. Cooper Pratt finally ended it by grounding out to third.
Wheeler, 36, is the 96th pitcher in major league history to reach 2,000 strikeouts and only nine got there faster.
It came almost a year after a surgeon in St. Louis removed his top rib to address the circulation problem in his arm.
The trouble started after a start in Washington on Aug. 15, 2025. Wheeler felt some heaviness in his right shoulder. By the next morning doctors had found a blood clot near it. The diagnosis was venous thoracic outlet syndrome, meaning a vein was getting pinched between his collarbone and rib cage. The fix was taking out the first rib and some of the muscle around it. He missed the rest of the season and the playoffs.
He came back April 25 against Atlanta, capped at 90 pitches. He hasn't looked back. Wheeler entered Tuesday 13-5 with a 2.99 ERA and 177 strikeouts in 150½ innings. In his previous four starts he had allowed three runs in 26 innings.
Aaron Nola still owns the Phillies' mark for strikeouts in a row at any point in a game. He struck out 10 straight Mets in June 2021, matching Tom Seaver's major league record from 1970. The modern record for starting a game that way is nine, set by Miami's Pablo Lopez against Atlanta in 2021.
Wheeler finished with 11 strikeouts Tuesday night in 5⅔ innings.

item.content:encoded:
Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. Oh, and he also grabbed hold of the American League lead in WAR back in July and still hasn’t relinquished it. A down year by Bobby Witt Jr.’s standards is still good enough to make him a deserving MVP.
I don’t know if Witt is going to win his first MVP this year. Ours is the only flavor of WAR in which he leads the AL, and he leads by just a quarter of a win. He ranks third by Baseball Reference’s rWAR and is eighth by Baseball Prospectus’ WARP. Yordan Alvarez leads all of baseball in WARP because he’s hitting like, well, Yordan Alvarez and staying healthy like, well, someone other than Yordan Alvarez. Cam Schlittler leads the AL in Baseball Reference WAR, and he’s been so dominant that he deserves consideration for the Cy Young-MVP combo — if only he’d pitched just 23 fewer innings last year, he could’ve gone for the trifecta with Rookie of the Year. Kevin McGonigle has played like an MVP from the moment he arrived in Detroit, and Junior Caminero has surpassed 40 home runs for the second season in a row as a 23-year-old. All of these guys have a case, and they aren’t the only ones who merit inclusion in the discussion:
| Name | fWAR Rk | fWAR | rWAR Rk | rWAR | WARP Rk | WARP | Avg Rk | Avg WAR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bobby Witt Jr. | 1 | 6.6 | 3 | 6.5 | 8 | 5 | 4 | 6.0 |
| Yordan Alvarez | 2 | 6.4 | 4 | 6.4 | 1 | 7.3 | 2 | 6.7 |
| Cam Schlittler | 3 | 6.1 | 1 | 7 | 3 | 5.8 | 2 | 6.3 |
| Dylan Cease | 4 | 5.5 | 8 | 5.7 | 12 | 4.6 | 8 | 5.3 |
| Miguel Vargas | 5 | 5.2 | 10 | 5.3 | 2 | 5.9 | 6 | 5.5 |
| Junior Caminero | 6 | 5.2 | 7 | 5.7 | 5 | 5.3 | 6 | 5.4 |
| Kevin McGonigle | 7 | 5.1 | 2 | 6.7 | 4 | 5.3 | 4 | 5.7 |
| Randy Arozarena | 8 | 5.1 | 11 | 5.3 | 16 | 4 | 12 | 4.8 |
| Dillon Dingler | 9 | 4.6 | 25 | 4 | 23 | 3.3 | 19 | 4.0 |
| Drew Rasmussen | 10 | 4.6 | 21 | 4.2 | 13 | 4.4 | 15 | 4.4 |
| Reid Detmers | 11 | 4.6 | 35 | 3.7 | 11 | 4.7 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Parker Messick | 13 | 4.6 | 6 | 5.8 | 9 | 4.8 | 9 | 5.1 |
| Pete Alonso | 14 | 4.2 | 18 | 4.3 | 6 | 5.3 | 13 | 4.6 |
| Ceddanne Rafaela | 21 | 3.9 | 9 | 5.4 | 94 | 1.7 | 41 | 3.7 |
| Gavin Williams | 27 | 3.7 | 46 | 3.1 | 7 | 5.2 | 27 | 4.0 |
| Wilyer Abreu | 32 | 3.4 | 5 | 5.8 | 20 | 3.6 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Mike Trout | 40 | 3.2 | 28 | 3.9 | 10 | 4.8 | 26 | 4.0 |
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, Schlittler, McGonigle and JJ Wetherholt have made the AL MVP the only major award that’s really in question). If you want to read a particularly good example, you should check out the one Mario Delgado Genzor wrote for Baseball Prospectus on Friday. I want to focus on something slightly different — namely, how good Witt has already been in years when he missed out on an MVP and how unusual it would be for him to win it this year.
(A quick note before we get into it: We’re about to spend a lot of time talking about WAR. I know I mentioned rWAR and WARP earlier. They’re an important piece of the puzzle, especially due to the outsized effect rWAR in particular has on the MVP conversation, but from here on out, we’re sticking with good old FanGraphs WAR.)
This is Witt’s fifth major league season, and you could argue that it’s his fourth consecutive MVP-caliber campaign. Mind you, that argument would focus only on 2022, in which he put up 5.9 WAR, good for 10th in the majors. There’s no argument to be had about the 2024 and 2025 seasons. That said, along with Shohei Ohtani’s combined 9.2-WAR 2022 sesaon, they are the two most valuable seasons this decade for which a position player did not win an MVP. In 2024, Witt ran a 169 wRC+, stole 31 bases, and put up a Fielding Run Value of 11, fourth among all shortstops. That was good for 10.5 WAR, and it took the best season of Aaron Judge’s career – 58 home runs, a 19% walk rate, and a .322 batting average – to beat him. In 2025, Witt put up 8.0 WAR with a 130 wRC+, 38 steals, and 20 FRV, the best mark among all shortstops. Again, he was bested by a 10-win season from Judge and Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer campaign. Witt has never received a first place MVP vote.
Crow-Armstrong, who has the National League MVP all but locked down, gives us a great example of what it normally takes to win an MVP award. He may even finish with 10.5 WAR through his excellence in all three phases of the game, just like Witt did in 2024. Players like Judge, Ohtani, and Mike Trout, whose base level of talent is so high that a healthy campaign is almost sure to keep them a step above the rest of the league, don’t come around all that often. Even when they do come around, they still need to be playing at something close to their peak, and peaks don’t last that long. Until Ohtani, the only player to win more than three MVPs was Barry Bonds, whose regimen for raising and widening his peak has been well documented. Sometimes that’s because of voter fatigue, but often it’s because somebody else popped up with an amazing, undeniable season like PCA’s. Most of the time, the MVP is an already great player for whom everything goes perfectly. They stay healthy and they play not just their best, but over their heads. Think of Ronald Acuña Jr. winning the NL MVP in 2023 with 9.1 WAR, 4.1 more than his next-best total, or Mookie Betts winning the AL MVP in 2018 with 10.2 WAR, 2.8 more than his next-best total.
Generally speaking, since the voting started getting more rigorous in the last couple decades, those are the two categories of players who win MVPs. We see all-time greats who perform like only they are capable of performing, and we see excellent players who put it all together in a blaze of glory. Witt’s 2024 season probably falls into that second category. He wasn’t quite at his defensive or baserunning peak, but he put up his best season at the plate by nearly 40 points of wRC+ and DRC+, and he ended up with an all-timer of a season. His 10.5 WAR tied for the 36th-best position player campaign of all time. His company? Willie Mays and Babe Ruth twice apiece, Barry Bonds, and Rogers Hornsby. Unfortunately, he ran into one of those special players from the first category, in the form of Judge. If Witt had put up those 2024 numbers this year, he’d be en route to a unanimous MVP just like PCA.
But I said “in theory” earlier, and I said it because Witt isn’t done yet. He’s still just 26, and if not for those weeks he missed with back tightness, or a wOBA that’s more than 30 points below his xwOBA, he’d now be wrapping up his third straight seven-plus-win season. He’s elite in every facet of the game and he doesn’t look like he’s in danger of slowing down any time soon. It wouldn’t be much of a shock to see him rediscover his nine- or 10-win form. In other words, there’s at least a chance Witt belongs to that first category of player and not the second.
Earlier I mentioned Acuña and Betts claiming MVPs by putting up the best years of their careers by a long shot. That’s pretty standard. Especially in recent years, it’s awfully rare for a player to take home an MVP award in something other than the best season of their career, unless they also won the MVP in the best year of their career. Leaving those multi-time MVPs out (and excluding 2020 for obvious reasons), here’s the whole list of players who won an MVP in a year that wasn’t their best by fWAR since 2011: Giancarlo Stanton and Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt put up 6.8 WAR in his 2022 NL MVP season and 7.2 in 2015. In that sense, Goldschmidt fit a third archetype: the established star who doesn’t put up their biggest WAR total, and instead wins MVP as something of a career achievement award. Stanton put up 6.5 WAR in 2017, not quite the 6.8-win campaign he put up in 2014, but he was facing a weaker field, he was more established as a star, and he had the cachet of a 59-homer season. We’re talking about gaps of less than half a win. We had some multi-time winners, but Acuña, Betts, Cody Bellinger, Christian Yelich, Jose Altuve, Kris Bryant, Josh Donaldson, Andrew McCutchen, and Buster Posey all won MVP in the best seasons of their career by fWAR.
Let’s say that Witt does win the MVP this year. For the sake of round numbers, let’s say he closes strong and finishes with 7.0 WAR. That would be just the third-best season of his career, and a full 3.5 WAR below his career-high. Baseball Reference lists MVP winners going back to 1911, and in that time, Witt would become just the ninth position player to win MVP in a season that trailed their best year by such a wide margin. The list of players to do it before him is full of three-time MVPs like Joe DiMaggio, Mickey Mantle, and Mike Schmidt. Not only that, but you’ll note that if Witt does make this list, the only higher number in either column will belong to Mantle:
| Player | MVP Year | MVP WAR | Best Year | Best WAR | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frankie Frisch | 1931 | 4.1 | 1927 | 9.7 | 5.6 |
| Mickey Mantle | 1962 | 6.0 | 1956 | 11.5 | 5.5 |
| Willie Stargell | 1979 | 2.7 | 1971 | 8.2 | 5.4 |
| Joe DiMaggio | 1947 | 4.8 | 1941 | 9.7 | 4.9 |
| Freddie Freeman | 2020* | 3.0 | 2023 | 7.7 | 4.7 |
| Robin Yount | 1989 | 5.3 | 1982 | 9.8 | 4.5 |
| Andre Dawson | 1987 | 3.5 | 1982 | 7.3 | 3.8 |
| Mike Schmidt | 1986 | 5.8 | 1974 | 9.4 | 3.6 |
| Roger Peckinpaugh | 1925 | 2.4 | 1919 | 5.9 | 3.5 |
The last person to do so was Robin Yount, who won the AL MVP with 9.8 WAR in 1982, and then again with 5.3 WAR in 1989, long before anybody knew that Total Zone considered him the 11th-worst defender in the majors. This hasn’t happened in nearly 30 years, and Witt is in a very different boat here. He’s not one of the two MVP favorites because his season looks great to the eye but doesn’t fool the advanced metrics. He’s not an aging star who can count on some lifetime-achievement votes. He’s a young gun who’s leading his league in WAR because he excels in every facet of the game.
I realize that this is far from the most meticulous analysis I’ve ever conducted, and that MVP voting is and should be about more than WAR. Still, I hope I’ve put this season in the context it deserves. By our measuring stick, Witt has been the best player in the American League this season. He’s done so despite missing time due to injury. He’s done so despite some bad batted ball luck. And he’s done so despite not even coming close to the highest gear we know he’s got available to him, because that gear is so high that it’s normally reserved for inner-circle Hall of Famers. However the voting goes, Witt’s been in MVP form for three or four years now.
Davy Andrews is a Brooklyn-based musician and a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @davyandrewsdavy.bsky.social.

Judging from the roster for today's game, Gary Sanchez is coming in while Yelich comes out. William Contreras moves to designated hitter to make room for Sanchez.
Yelich is a 34-year-old slugger, while Sanchez is a 33-year-old catcher for the Brewers.
Looking At Christian Yelich & Gary Sanchez
Yelich is a 14-year MLB veteran who has been with the Brewers for nine seasons.
Over his career, he has been an All-Star several times, culminating in an NL MVP award in 2018. Yelich has enjoyed a solid 2026 campaign, notching 101 hits, 57 RBIs, 11 stolen bases, and 11 home runs in 112 games.
On the other hand, Sanchez has 44 hits, 35 RBIs, and 11 home runs in 83 games.
Pat Murphy on Christian Yelich
Recently, the Brewers manager has discussed Yelich's work ethic and his dedication to the game.
"I just remember he was here one night till 1 o'clock in the morning. A lot of guys in his situation, you've won MVP, you've been an all-star multiple times, you've done all the things in the game, you are 12 years in your career, and you know what: he still cares so much about the Milwaukee Brewers. That's the beauty of this whole thing…you have no idea how much this guy cares," Murphy said via a social media clip from Hunter Baumgardt.
